subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING EMERGENCY MEASURES ORGANIZATION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Righl Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement in connection with the emergency measures organization. Hon. members will recall that some months ago the government adopted the policy of arranging for regional, federal administration in Canada should a major war occur, to work in co-operation with provincial governments and tie in with the regional army commands.
The plan is to provide in each province a centre from which a small core of federal, provincial and army personnel can direct emergency operations within the province, even in the presence of radioactive fall-out, the loss of normal means of communication and possibly the destruction of some provincial capitals.
Continuity of government is essential to our survival as a nation, and the need of guidance and control by civilian authority will be more than ever vital to our people should Canada find itself in war. Moreover, the army has responsibility for emergency communications, for the attack warning system, for prediction of fall-out patterns, and for a number of other important survival services. These responsibilities make it necessary to have a centre in each province where, given reasonable protection against fall-out, the army can meet its military commitments and carry out the survival and support functions it has been assigned.
The government, in assessing physical requirements for meeting the federal civilian responsibilities and for those falling on the army, believes that they should be met from the same emergency centre in each province, recognizing as it does the very important role of the provinces in respect of the more localized wartime responsibilities falling on them. While the regional governmental centres will be provided and administered by federal authorities, the plan is to make suitable provision for a nucleus of the provincial government and officials in each regional centre. In this way the province concerned would use the facilities there to aid in meeting
its own wartime role, and would work in close association with federal authorities in so doing.
Regional centres will be established speedily in each of the provinces. There will be some variation in their size and character, depending on a number of factors including the size of the population to be served, the likelihood of the provincial capital coming under direct attack, and particularly the emergency communications system and its technical requirements. The centres will be limited in size but will be sufficient to ensure the required operational capability.
In some provinces construction will be necessary, while in others modification of existing buildings may suffice to meet the requirement. The principal need is adequate protection against radioactive fall-out, the same peril against which the government is encouraging householders to protect themselves by means of suitable basement shelters. Immediate action is being taken to provide the required structures, and details regarding provincial participation in their use will be the subject of discussion with provincial authorities forthwith.
In making this announcement at the present time, Mr. Speaker, I underline and emphasize what I said on an earlier occasion when this plan had its inception, namely that I do not want anyone to interpret the announcement at this time as indicative of any change in the peaceful relationship of our country with other countries.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have that correction made by the minister in the record of what he said yesterday, but I am afraid it does not alter my feeling about this bill as being one that we on this side will not be able to support on second reading.
Last evening I was trying to correct the historical background to this bill as it was put forward by the minister. This afternoon I should like to begin my remarks by saying something about the events leading up to the bill itself. Those events represent another instance of fumbling and indecision on the part of the minister and the government.
For more than two years the minister has been talking about changes to the Combines Investigation Act. He discussed the principles involved in some detail in 1958. He discussed them again in January, 1959 in a speech he made in New York. But the bill which was to have dealt with this matter was not introduced into this house until June 11, 1959. We recall that it was introduced at that time without a preceding resolution, an omission which was surprising on the part of a minister who is such an expert on the rules; therefore a clause in the bill last year which provided for the appointment of ad hoc commissioners had to be deleted. On June 15, 1959, four days after the introduction of the bill, we had another speech on the question by the minister in Montreal, this time dealing with the matters which were contained in the bill. In a sense this was the minister's second reading speech on the amendments of last year, although the speech was made in Montreal. However, consideration of the bill in the house was delayed, because it became evident very quickly that the bill was ill conceived and highly objectionable and, as I think the minister himself admitted last night, some 79951-0-275
Combines Investigation Act strong protests concerning it were received. Therefore some parts of the bill were, I think rightly, withdrawn on July 7 before any consideration could have been given to it, presumably because of the representations which were received.
At that time, however, the minister decided to proceed with the amendments to the resale price maintenance sections of the act; then later he decided to withdraw that part of the bill as well. Now, one year later, and four months after the beginning of this session, we have for consideration this other bill which in some of its provisions at least is new, and so we ask ourselves why this indecision, why this hesitation, why these changes and this chopping; and we will do our best to find out about that in committee.
The history of this matter, as I tried to point out last night, and the background to the introduction of this bill both reflect the fact that the positions of the two parties on this subject are basically different. The position of the Liberal party historically has been that competition should be maintained and enforced in the private sector of our economy. The position of the Conservative party over the years has been in favour of the regulation of competition even if this should mean certain combines, monopolies or restrictive practices, if they were found not to be against the public interest. In other words the Conservative party has not shown itself to be as keen about competition within the private sector of our economy as it has always shown itself to be keen about competition between public and private enterprise. The present bill, as I shall try to point out, reflects this attitude.
The fact is that our economy, as I also tried to point out last night in brief, whatever may have been the situation 100 years ago, has altered. Today it is quite unrealistic to describe the Canadian economy without qualification as a private enterprise economy. What we have is a mixed economy with public, co-operative and private enterprise sectors, and this is as it should be. For progress and for stability the government has had to accept increasing responsibilities in the public sector to fight unemployment, for instance, and inflation. Private or free enterprise alone could not possibly do this job. Moreover, there are certain undertakings and certain national activities which must be assigned to public initiative if we wish to ensure the greatest possible freedom and welfare for the individual.
However, the scope and nature of this kind of government intervention will vary in different countries, and it will vary at different stages of development in the same

Combines Investigation Act country. Similarly the co-operative sector which is growing in importance in our country, and rightly so, has a great part to play in ensuring the prosperity and progress of the small producers and consumers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question there. I would be interested to know whether in his use of the word "co-operative", which he also used last night, the Leader of the Opposition refers to co-operative organizations in the generally accepted sense or wnether, as might have been suggested, he means an area of co-operation between public enterprise and private enterprise?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
While of course, Mr. Speaker, there should be co-operation between public and private enterprise in their respective sectors of the economy, I was using the word "co-operative" in the sense the minister mentioned, as referring to co-operative undertakings within our economy.
We accept, as Liberals, that these two divisions exist, but as Liberals we also believe there is a large and important sector of the economy which should be left to private enterprise for exactly the same reasons I have mentioned in connection with the other two, the progress, prosperity and freedom of the individual. All these considerations require what I have called a mixed economy, each sector serving the public interest in its own way and according to rules laid down. In considering this bill we are particularly considering the rules that should be laid down.
That is our view, and it opposes the traditional Conservative insistence on extreme private enterprise and the socialist insistence on extreme public enterprise. These differences are bound to lead to different approaches as between the parties to the problem of monopoly. We believe, for instance, that if the private sector of the economy is to best serve the public interest it should be subject to the maximum possible extent to the competitive rule. Private controls within that sector will certainly be inadequate. Public regulation of private initiative is a poor substitute for competition as a preventive of monopoly, and it tends at times to serve the private rather than the public interest. In our view-and I think history supports that view-the traditional attitude of the Conservative party has been otherwise. In the past they have encouraged the development of private controls and privileges and weakened the competitive rule in many fields of economic activity.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that attitude continues to be shown in some sections of this bill,


which we oppose. As I ventured to point out very briefly last night, without changing the legislation that we have now in any respect, by administrative action it could be improved in three ways. Perhaps I might go into those possible changes in more detail this afternoon. First-and this is one I mentioned last night-the powers of investigation of the director, which are wide and rightly so, should obviously not be abused and should obviously be used with discretion. They should always be carried out on the presumption that anyone, a corporation or an individual, is innocent until he or it is proven guilty.
I recognize that last night the minister complained that I had charged that there have been complaints on this score. I feel, and I am quite willing to repeat my feeling in the house, that the attitude and conduct of investigation by the investigators should be scrupulously fair to those investigated, with strict administrative directives to ensure against any possible abuse of power; otherwise, as I already said, public confidence in the act will be weakened.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the MacQuarrie committee, which has been mentioned already more than once, recommended that the commission in its hearings and reports should not always make those reports preliminary to criminal prosecution, because the present law does say that such a report shall "appraise the effect on the public interest of arrangements and practices disclosed in the evidence and contain recommendations as to the application of remedies provided in this act" and then it adds these three words "or other remedies"; other remedies such as the use of tariffs or the use of patent legislation.
Convictions and penalties are not always the best or the only remedies to correct an undesirable monopolistic situation or practice. I take it that when the trade practices commission was set up it was expected to recommend such other remedies as it could find to correct undesirable practices, and it has not done so.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not being critical of the commission for that, because during the three years of the activity of the commission on restrictive trade practices, under the present government, there have been only two members on the commission; the third member, I think, was appointed only recently. Before that time this commission, which was not appointed very many years ago, felt it had quite enough to do-and indeed it had more than enough to do, as I perhaps will be able to point out when I come to another change that may be suggested; yet I express the hope that in the future it will be able to use more than it has in the past this provision for other remedies, to quote the act.
Then a third change which I hope can be made, and which does not require any alteration of the present legislation, is to strengthen and intensify the work of the commission in research in the field of monopolistic situations. The minister will remember, of course, that the MacQuarrie committee put great emphasis on research of this kind, and it had a good deal to say in its report about the importance of these matters of research.
Section 42 of the act, as amended in 1952, implemented the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee in this regard and gave wide powers of research to the director. That will be found on pages 55 and 56 of the report. But these powers have not been exercised to any significant extent; and if that is the case again I say, Mr. Speaker, it is not the director's fault, because his staff is small and more skilled research personnel are needed for this work of investigation, which seems to me of such great importance to the effective operation of this office. The provision of that kind of help, of course, is the responsibility of the government. If a greater effort could be made in this field and provision for this effort made we would surely have a far better knowledge and a far greater understanding of monopoly problems than we have now; what steps should be taken to correct them, and what changes are needed in the present legislation.
These are three changes that could be made in the present legislation without amending the act at all. However, we have before us a bill which does introduce amendments to the act. Dealing with the bill itself and the principles embodied in it, Mr. Speaker, I recall that the minister said last night-I may not be quoting him exactly, but I am sure this is the meaning of what he said-that this bill recognizes the inherent soundness of the principles of the present legislation. If that is true, then of course this bill in intention at least does not change those principles; but as we read it, as we 79951-0-275i
Combines Investigation Act understand the amendments, they will certainly weaken the principle which is inherent in the present legislation. We cannot see in this bill, whatever its purpose may be, any result which would protect either small business or the consumer. We think the effect of this bill will be to weaken competition, to give more rather than less protection to combines, and to reintroduce undesirable monopolistic practices.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I shall try to produce evidence to support the contention. The minister pointed out last night that there are two main parts to the bill. There is the part dealing with monopolistic situations, and there is the part dealing with trade practices. As he did, I should like to deal with these in turn.
The part dealing with monopolistic situations can be divided into changes recommended regarding definitions, changes in regard to litigation procedure and remedies, and new remedies to be applied. Let us look at the changes in definition first. The definition of monopoly in the amendment is substantially the same as it was, and the test remains operation to the detriment or against the interest of the public. In the case of mergers this test is restricted by the qualification that competition must be lessened. While the detrimental aspects of most mergers are to be found in the lessening of competition, there are others which might involve broader considerations of public interest; and since mergers often give rise to monopolies it seems to us that the same tests and the same definition should be applied to both as is the case under the present law.
There are also some changes proposed in the definition of a combine or conspiracy, and these are important. With two modifications, one of which may be a little more important than it may seem on the surface, the bill incorporates section 411 of the Criminal Code, that section which defines conspiracy, as the minister pointed out. We on this side have no great objection to putting that section of the Criminal Code in the Combines Investigation Act. But what is more serious is a new and broad exemption under the bill. Under a provision of the bill a combine relating to certain matters -the minister mentioned what they were last night-such as exchange of statistics, definition of product standards, research and one or two other things, may operate provided it has not lessened or is not likely to lessen competition unduly in respect of the five matters which we both mentioned last night; prices, quantity or quality of production, markets or customers, channels or methods

Combines Investigation Act
of distribution, and restriction from entering into or expanding in an industry. Therefore under this provision these practices on this condition-I add that-will be permitted. That is a substantial departure from the principles of traditional legislation in this field. If combinations are allowed for these purposes, would other agreements be necessary to eliminate competition with respect to prices or production or markets? There are a great many objective experts, students of this subject, who have studied these matters carefully and who think the answer to that question would be in the negative.
I realize, of course, that an agreement even on the matters enumerated will be illegal if the courts find that it has lessened or is likely to lessen competition unduly in respect of the matters I have mentioned. Nevertheless the minister will agree that this is an entirely new test for the courts. Proceedings before the courts in this field up to now have been relatively simple, though some people might not consider them absolutely simple. It has to be shown that an arrangement regarding prices or production does exist and that it involves substantial control over the market for the product concerned. That is all. Therefore the evidence is or needs to be largely limited to matters of fact, namely the existence of an agreement and the degree of control brought about by that agreement in the industry in question.
Under this amendment the task of the courts will be much more complicated. They will still have to make findings as to the existence of an agreement and the degree of control; but also, in relation to the matters and practices enumerated, the courts will now have to appraise the effects of such arrangements on prices, production, markets, distribution and the number of units in an industry and find, if they can, whether in these respects competition will be lessened unduly by any arrangement made.
How will the courts decide whether an arrangement about the exchange of statistics on costs and prices, an exchange of figures on costs and prices, will lessen competition unduly in respect of prices? Will it be on the basis of mere uniformity of prices? The minister knows that in economic theory prices are also uniform under conditions of perfect and free competition. Will the courts then have to appraise the levels of prices, which would bring them into very intricate economic theories of evaluation?
Surely it has always been the prevailing view that the courts of our land were not well equipped to appraise the effects and consequences of trade practices of this kind. Mr. Justice Hope, one of the men learned in

the law of this country, in dealing with this matter once in a case had this to say:
The courts should not be called upon to adjudicate between conflicting theories of political economy.
Under these amendments they may well be called upon to do just that. I know that certain business groups, as the minister pointed out last night, I think, have complained about the uncertainty and vagueness of the present legislation. It is our contention that these amendments will make that situation more uncertain and more vague. How can these amendments improve the situation? Certain business groups have also requested -I think the Canadian Manufacturers' Association might be mentioned in this regard-[DOT] that certain joint activities or arrangements should be specifically legalized, and no doubt their briefs have had some effect on the minister. But how can this be done under amendments of this type without restricting the scope of the legislation as a whole? In any event, the bill provides only for conditional exemption, so that it even fails to meet the position that business groups have in mind because it does, as we see it, leave the position more uncertain and more vague, not more certain and more precise.
Under this bill even an arrangement for the exchange of official statistics could be brought under prosecution. Therefore while the bill is not going to help in this respect it does have some dangerous implications. As I have said, the courts will have to appraise the effects of a great variety of joint activities and consider in each case whether or not a specific detriment is involved. That is going to be very difficult for them. Either the courts will interpret this new provision, if it becomes law, so as to leave the existing jurisprudence unchanged, which would make the new provision useless, or they will interpret it as giving more leeway to business to engage in joint activities or combinations, which will greatly weaken our present legislation.
May I say a word, Mr. Speaker, about the second part of this section, concerning litigation procedure, and perhaps I can deal with remedies at the same time. Until 1952 the only litigation procedure for an offence was criminal procedure, criminal prosecution. It will be recalled that in its report the Mac-Quarrie committee expressed the view that it would be desirable if the courts had the statutory power to issue a judicial restraining order as a preventive procedure. But while they made that recommendation they apparently had some doubts about the constitutional validity of such a change, because at pages 40 and 41 of their report we find these words:

Already the courts have certain procedures of a preventive kind in the field of criminal law. Their power to bind over persons to keep the peace and to release persons upon the condition of future good behaviour approximate an injunctive process. There is as well, a growing body of doctrine that the courts have jurisdiction to issue orders preventing the commission of public wrongs ... Constitutionally a strong case can be made that federal jurisdiction over criminal law includes steps essential to the prevention of crime and that the authorities should not have to stand idly by until wrong has been done if the situation lends itself to preventive measures.
They are not too sure about the constitutionality, but they think it is arguable. They did, then, make this recommendation, and as a result the legislation was amended by a new subsection which provided for a restraining order. I am now talking about the existing legislation and not about the bill before us. The provision for a restraining order was only where, and I quote, "a person is about to do or is likely to do any act constituting... an offence". This new remedy, therefore, was limited and was not an alternative but a supplement to criminal prosecution. Under the present legislation, if an offence had been committed criminal prosecution remained the only procedure under the act.
This has been changed in this bill. Under this bill in proceedings commenced by information of the attorney general, the use of restraining orders is extended to cases where an offence has already been committed, and in such cases the court will merely prohibit the continuation of the offence. Moreover, this bill also provides that the attorney general may at his discretion-I mentioned those words last night as important-institute proceedings either by way of information or by way of prosecution.
This, Mr. Speaker, is new and it is a dangerous provision because it provides not a mere supplement but an alternative to criminal prosecution. If this bill is approved the minister will be in a position, at his own discretion, to institute proceedings for the same kind of offence either by way of information or by way of prosecution. In the latter case persons involved will have to go through a criminal trial, and in the former case they will not. If the prosecution resulted in a conviction they would be liable to two years' imprisonment or a heavy fine; but if the minister proceeds by information, at the most they would get a warning not to offend again and undo, if possible, what had been done.
This extension of the use of the restraining order, therefore, as an alternative to prosecution is, I repeat, a dangerous innovation. First, it is of dubious constitutionality as a civil remedy while federal jurisdiction in the
Combines Investigation Act field is limited to criminal action. Second, it involves undesirable discrimination in that different persons are liable to different treatment for the same offence at the minister's discretion; let us not get away from that. Finally, the new procedure will remove some of the risk of criminal procedure and punishment and therefore induce the formation of combines or even mergers and monopolies. This will decrease the preventive value of the present legislation. Nothing the minister said last night on second reading has removed our anxiety about the effect of these provisions.
The final part of this act, on the principle of which I want to say something, deals with trade practices. In this regard the bill refers to discrimination, trade allowances, price misrepresentation, matters which we will be able to discuss in some detail later in this debate or perhaps in committee. I am going to restrict my remarks at this time to one matter dealt with under this section, the matter of resale price maintenance, as it is affected by this bill.
There is a great deal of literature on this subject, and I am sure the minister has read much of it. I know it is a difficult and' complicated matter. I know there can be differences of opinion about it. But I know also that the MacQuarrie committee made an exhaustive examination of this whole question of resale price maintenance in 1951. The committee defined resale price maintenance-and I think it is an acceptable definition-at page 71 of their report as:
The practice designed to ensure that a particular article shall not be resold to retailers, wholesalers or other distributors at less than the price prescribed by the suppliers, that is, in most cases the manufacturers.
After the examination which they gave to this matter the committee came to the conclusion that resale price maintenance was not justified, either on the ground of economic efficiency or of maintaining a free, competitive economy; or, indeed, on the ground of protecting the small businessman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman say again from what page he read that definition?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, it is the definition in the 1951 interim report of the MacQuarrie committee on resale price maintenance. It is on page 71 of that interim report, I think that is the correct reference. This committee viewed resale price maintenance, and I quote again from its report, as-
-a manifestation of a restrictive or monopolistic practice which does not promote the general welfare.
It also condemned these practices for other reasons. I am going to read some of the
4368	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act reasons which were given in this report; because while the minister claims that resale price maintenance is not affected by these amendments, since it is retained in the legislation, it is our contention that because of the provisions in the legislation dealing with loss leaders it will now be greatly affected. These are the reasons given against it by the MacQuarrie committee:
1.	The direct and immediate effect of resale price maintenance is the elimination of price competition among retailers in price-maintained goods; ...
2.	Resale price maintenance facilitates and makes more effective horizontal agreements (open or tacit) among manufacturers ...
3.	Resale price maintenance, to be effective, requires some method of enforcement. If a manufacturer merely indicates a resale price but makes no provision and takes no step to enforce it, then he has no real control over his distributors. However, when measures of enforcement are involved, resale price maintenance establishes a private system of law allowing no appeal to the courts of justice ...
If these amendments are passed it is our contention that this would be done.
4.	Although precise information is lacking, there is some evidence that resale price maintenance contributes to price stability but that the general level of prices thus stabilized is higher than it would be under competitive conditions and production more unstable.
These reasons are given on pages 67 and 68 of this interim report. Acting on these recommendations, Mr. Speaker, the previous government, at the end of 1951, introduced amendments to the Combines Investigation Act-after a great deal of care and consideration and after this exhaustive examination by an objective, impartial committee, not in haste and not without consideration- designed to implement the recommendations of this committee report and to prohibit resale price maintenance. After a long debate and very strong opposition led by the opposition party of that day, in which the present minister took a very leading part, the amendment was finally approved by parliament.
There were dire predictions at that time that at the first possible opportunity this amendment would be removed by a Conservative government when it came into office. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is our contention that this amendment we have before us, or a provision in it, does undo what was done in 1951 under the provision for dealing with loss leaders.
Now, this practice of loss leaders was dealt with in this report as well, and was also very thoroughly investigated by the director of investigation and research and by the restrictive trade practices commission.
It was investigated for over two years, in fact for nearly two and a half years. As a result of this investigation, which was


thorough, capable and objective, in March, 1955 the commission issued a report which included a unanimous conclusion that no legislative steps should be taken against loss leaders. In brief the reasons given-and they will be found at pages 265 and 266 of the commission report of March, 1955 on this subject-were that the retailing difficulties which the commission realized existed at that time were not caused by this practice of loss leaders but by changes brought about by the action of normal competitive forces in our economy.
Here, Mr. Speaker, after an impartial and exhaustive inquiry, a commission recommended that no change should be made in the law, and after it heard individuals and groups who were interested in the question. I ask the minister these questions. Did he seek the advice of this commission before deciding to change the law? Was there an investigation before these amendments were decided on by the government? Was an investigation or inquiry made under section 42(1) of the present legislation? Did the director act on his own initiative in making any such investigation, or was he instructed by the minister to do so, or did the restrictive trade practices commission make such an investigation? Our answers to these questions on this side must presumably be no, because no report has been made as is required by the act. Therefore presumably no investigation was made. Therefore the minister failed to follow the proper procedure to investigate these practices mentioned in clause 14 of the bill before he introduced legislation to curb them.
The last inquiry or the last investigation that was made reported against such a change. Surely that makes the neglect of the minister to order such an inquiry the more reprehensible.

speechtext:
There are five conditions in the bill, two of which deal with exactly the same thing, as I have shown. If the minister wants me to read all five in all their detail I shall be glad to do so. However, I have given my four, one of which includes two in the bill. What kind of evidence will justify the supplier to take action under this clause? The supplier will be the judge; he will decide. In order to be entitled to refuse to sell he will not have to show that the retailer did in fact engage in the practices enumerated in the bill. He will only have to indicate that he and an informer-possibly a competitor of the so-called accused-had reasonable cause to believe and did believe that the retailer was following those practices.
4370	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act
Mr. Speaker, that surely is a travesty of justice, if you can use that word at all in relation to it. The informer, that is the man giving the information, who as I say might well be a competitor of the retailer, will need to have very little evidence indeed to have reasonable cause to believe that his competitor was following those practices which are so vaguely described in this bill. A manufacturer or supplier could be bombarded by a multitude of informers wishing to eliminate their competitors, and might find himself in a quite untenable position. Indeed, he would have to examine the representations received from any such informers and decide on the basis of the information he received whether he had reasonable cause to believe that the accused retailer did engage in those practices. He will not only have to make decisions on the basis of the reports received from the informers, but he will also have to be in a position to defend such decisions before the courts.
Mr. Speaker, we are therefore creating the fantastic situation where retailers could police and denounce each other, and where the manufacturer would find himself in the position of a judge between them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman realizes, of course, that there is no obligation on the manufacturer to do that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course there is no obligation; let me make that clear. What I am suggesting is what might very well happen, if this bill becomes law, in manufacturing and in retailing. If it does happen, how can the manufacturer be considered an impartial judge? He will obviously be an interested party to the transaction, and he will not be forced under the law to take any action of any kind against any retailer. Therefore he may use the powers conferred upon him-and they are important powers-in a discriminatory fashion, or he may not use them at all. He may cut off supplies to Smith but permit Jones to conduct the very same practices. He is not obliged to do anything, which would make it much easier for him to discriminate. Surely this power is subversive of fair dealing and equal opportunity for all, and could be used as a weapon to control the distribution of a product in a wrong and discriminatory fashion. If it cannot be used for that purpose, I would be interested to hear the minister remove our doubts on that matter.
The supplier, then, will not be, and could not very well be on the face of it, an impartial and objective judge. He will also not be a free judge. Indeed, retailers will resent price cutting by a competitor more than the supplier himself might. They can exercise,


either individually or through their trade association, very strong pressure on the supplier and threaten to refuse to handle his product if he does not take action against the price cutter. Such pressures and threats will be, of course, reasonable cause to believe that he is entitled to refuse to sell.
In addition, the accusations which the supplier-that is the judge-has to believe before being entitled to impose a penalty are at best expressed in very vague terms indeed. In so far as the meaning of some of those accusations can be ascertained, they refer to practices which can hardly be viewed as detrimental in themselves to the public interest.
Mr. Speaker, let us look at the four or five of them, whichever you wish. The first two are, if I may abbreviate the definitions, selling "for the purpose of advertising" and "of attracting customers".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I suggest again that the hon. gentleman complete that particular quotation, which is "in the hope of selling them other articles". I think it is important to have the whole definition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would be happy to do that. The first one is this, subsection (a) of section 14:
(a)	that the other person was making a practice of using articles supplied by the person charged as loss leaders, that is to say, not for the purpose of making a profit thereon but for purposes of advertising;
The second one is:
(b)	that the other person was making a practice of using articles supplied by the person charged not for the purpose of selling such articles at a Drofit but for the purpose of attracting customers to his store in the hope of selling them other articles;
That, Mr. Speaker, is why I lumped these two together in effect as dealing with the same thing, and that is also why I made four out of the five provisions in the bill.
These first two practices which I have read in full are of course, substantially the same, so it is not clear, in my mind at least, why we should have two clauses at all.
The meaning of these clauses is quite clear. A seller may be exposed to retaliation by the supplier if he uses the article not for the purpose of making a profit thereon but for the purpose of advertising or of attracting customers to his store. Well, Mr. Speaker, surely the minister will admit that those expressions are very vague and susceptible of very different interpretations. A seller, for instance, may decide to reduce the price of an item below the prevailing level for the purpose of increasing his volume of business while still making a profit, a little less profit, per article. However, if he resorts to that device, under

this amendment he would be using the article for purposes of advertising or of attracting customers to his store and not for the purpose of making a profit, which in this particular case would be a secondary consideration. He would also be liable under the clause to have the supplier cut him off.
Now, on what basis will the supplier decide that the article was not sold for the purpose of making a profit and that such selling, not for the purpose of making a profit, had become a practice? It would be almost impossible for the supplier to make his decision on refusal to sell on a precise mark-up or cost, including the handling cost of the seller, because mark-ups and costs vary from one article to another and under reasonably free competition vary from one retailer to another. Very often the retailer himself does not even know what his cost of handling a particular article may be, because he is primarily interested in the profit of his business as a whole.
If the retailer does not know exactly his own cost and profit per unit, how can the manufacturer or supplier be expected to know whether or not the retailer is making a profit or is selling the article for the purpose of making a profit, indulging in that as a practice? How will the supplier know what purpose the retailer had in mind?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: The supplier can read the invoice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, of course he can read the invoice, but that will not help the manufacturer in the application of this particular provision.
One method available to the supplier would be to take the average mark-up shown by the studies of the dominion bureau of statistics for the whole trade in question. He could insist that if his product is sold in a particular store below that mark-up, then it is not being sold for the purpose of making a profit thereon. That would not be a very satisfactory method.
Another method would be to suggest an acceptable price to the retailer or to all retailers in that line after consultation with the appropriate trade association, and to decide that any price below the suggested level indicated that the article was not sold for the purpose of making a profit; and if he so decides he could cut the retailer off.
These two methods, or some modification of them, which are the only ones I can think of which could be used by the supplier in arriving at a decision to sell or not to sell, will enable the manufacturer himself to enforce indirectly but very effectively a scheme of resale price maintenance.
