Combines Investigation Act
So we have resale price maintenance of this type enforced not by law but by the supplier. The very act which continues the prohibition in one of its clauses-resale price maintenance-by this particular amendment would be introducing or re-introducing that undesirable practice, as I have said, through the back door. Moreover, it will still be quite legitimate to spend millions on advertising "for the purpose of attracting customers" but a retailer will be liable to retaliation if he follows a continuing policy of "specials" to do the same thing. The big stores can, of course, spend millions in advertising but small stores cannot and price reductions are very often the only method available to them to compete with large scale advertising.
The fact is that this so-called ban on loss leaders, enforced not by the law but by the manufacturers, is not really going to hurt the chain stores, the big stores, or to help the small independent dealer. The chains and the big retailers have already shown in the experience of recent years that they are quite prepared to stick to resale prices on nationally known brands while cutting prices on their own widely known private brands, products it should be noted that are not available at all to the small retailer.
Then there is the provision, I think it is No. 3 in clause (c), which could be urged as a defence against prosecution under the resale price maintenance clause. According to the new provisions the supplier will also be able to refuse to sell if the retailer is persistently engaging in misleading advertising. I do not think anyone could take exception to that except that it puts powers in the hands of manufacturers to do something which should be and which indeed is illegal under the law and under this very act. I am therefore at a loss to understand why the minister should put it in this particular clause.
Then there is the failure to provide servicing which could be urged as a defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Servicing at certain levels.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister would like me to read the provision. This provision could be urged as a defence by the supplier:
(d) that the other person made a practice of not providing the level of servicing that purchasers of such articles might reasonably expect from such other person:
This is a new arbitrary power conferred upon the manufacturers in this country. The manufacturer, not the court, will be called upon to appraise what the purchasers might reasonably expect from the retailers in terms of servicing and if that hypothetical but reasonable expectation is not met he will be justified in refusing to sell to them. If he is

Combines Investigation Act accused of indulging in resale price maintenance he can urge this as a complete defence.
How can the manufacturer make an unbiased appraisal of consumers' expectations in regard to servicing? The minister must know-he is a consumer and perhaps a shopper too-that consumers' preferences vary in this matter perhaps more than in any other aspect of retailing. A great number of people prefer to buy a product at a lower price without any servicing attached to it. Others are willing to pay a higher price provided the cost of normal servicing during a given period is included in that price. We feel that the various preferences of consumers should be met on the market and that retailers should be free to meet those preferences according to the competitive rule and that no manufacturer should be able to urge as a defence against a breach of the law that some retailer was not giving adequate service as a practice to his customers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: He could only urge it if the retailer held himself out as giving a service and did not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Why not abide by the rules of the house?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have read that provision and although the meaning may not be clear the wording is very specific. I will now read the last chapter in this charter of commercial feudalism of 1960:
(e) that the other person was unfairly disparaging the value of articles supplied by the person charged, in relation to their price or otherwise.
In other words the supplier will be able to refuse to sell if the retailer is unfairly disparaging the value of articles sold to him. I wonder what is meant by that? What is meant by "unfairly disparaging the value of articles sold to him"? Of all the vague expressions in this bill, surely that is just about the vaguest.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: In other words, "Buy this thing; it's so lousy".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: It is claimed that consumers often judge the quality of a product by its price. A manufacturer, therefore, surely will have reasonable cause to believe that the value of his product is unfairly disparaged if it is sold by a retailer at a price below the prevailing price. The supplier will be entitled to refuse to sell if he believes that his product is not well located in the retailer's store or is not well presented by the dealer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: He can do that now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Is the minister trying to tell me that under our present law if a product
is not well shown in a retail store the manufacturer can cut the retailer off from that product under the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, certainly. There is no resale price maintenance there at all. That is not related to price.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: This is resale price maintenance-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: -by giving the manufacturer the right to cut the retailer off from his product if he has reasonable cause to believe that the value of his product is unfairly disparaged if it is sold by a retailer at a price below the prevailing price, or if the product is not shown or displayed as the manufacturer thinks he would like to see it displayed. He can urge this provision as a complete defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: As he can do now.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: If that is so, why is this provision necessary?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: If that is the case, why make the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: To make it clear. We have said that all along. Have you just discovered that? Have hon. gentlemen opposite just now found out what their own law means? No wonder they are surprised and amused.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is a new interpretation of the law. These particular clauses are for the purpose only of clarification according to the minister. If so, it is the vaguest kind of clarification that was ever introduced into any legislation. This gives the manufacturer wide discriminatory powers over the retailer's business. It can be expected perhaps that the powers will be exercised mainly against the small retailer and the dealers who are attempting to reduce the cost of distribution. Indeed, the lower the cost of handling a product the more likely will its value be disparaged, to use the language of the section. We contend, therefore, that this provision will endanger the independence of retailers, hit low-cost distributors more heavily than the others, and will certainly hurt the consumer.
Those are some of the reasons-and there are others which will be brought forward in the course of this debate-which I hope make it quite clear that we consider this bill retrogressive. We feel it will do harm rather than good to the small businessman and the small retailer and the consumer. Because of that we will certainly vote against second reading of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would the Leader of the Opposition permit one question before he leaves the subject of second reading. The

hon. gentleman said in the course of his remarks that surely there are better ways of helping small business than those represented by the amendments to section 34. I am sure it would be helpful if the hon. gentleman would indicate some of the ways of helping small business within the ambit of the combines legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, I will be glad to send the proposals to the minister. It would take me a long time to repeat the proposals we have made in the last four years to help small business, especially on the financial side, on the loan side. Those proposals, which I will be glad to send to the minister's office, will be found by him to be very, very impressive, indeed, in comparison with the measures taken by the present government which, the minister said last night, are working quietly. Those measures involved the transformation of the office, which already existed in the Department of Trade and Commerce, into the same office with a different name, with an official in charge. I think he has a clerk and a stenographer. I think we can do better than that, Mr. Speaker, and I would be glad to send the minister a long list of proposals we have made in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would direct his remarks to this legislation.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose one should have a feeling of trepidation in following the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in the intensive debate that each of them has entered into in respect of the bill. However, I do not approach it in that light, because I consider this to be not only the most important piece of legislation presented to us so far this session or, for that matter, which appears on the order paper which may be proceeded with later, but also the most important piece of legislation that we have seen introduced so far by this particular government in so far as its broad aspects are concerned and the impact it will have upon the economy and upon the consumer. Nevertheless, I expect I may run into the 40-minute time limit rule, as to deal adequately and fully with the incorrect interpretations, the illogical assumptions and the misinformed analogies given to us last evening by the Minister of Justice would certainly take more than 40 minutes. It would require more than that time to set the record straight and to clear up those particular interpretations and assumptions.
One thing that struck me right from the outset of the minister's remarks was his reference to the need for a royal commission to study thoroughly and completely whether 79951-0-276)
Combines Investigation Act or not there should be a complete revision of the act. Almost in the next breath he said that since the day he assumed office he started within his department a study of his particular act itself and almost three years later we see the results of that study. Normally one would think that a royal commission would not take longer than a three-year period to make a thorough, full and complete study of the act and whether there was any need to change it.
What would be even more beneficial would be the fact that a royal commission at least would make a public report, would go into details and explain as thoroughly as it could the reasons for the proposed changes which it might suggest. Here we have the results of an interdepartmental study, with the report being secret or hidden, not available. We do not even know whether this proposed legislation before us now even meets with the approval of the people within the investigation branch itself. From reading reports of the restrictive trade practices commission over the years and prior to that by the director I would come to the conclusion that it does not represent fully the thoughts and ideas of the departmental officials responsible for this particular piece of legislation.
As I listened attentively to the minister last evening I was reminded of the first venture I made a few years ago to purchase a used car. I remember the salesman spending a great deal of time telling me how this used car was in reality a most outstanding car; that is, it had been tuned up, altered, changed, put in tune with the times. In fact, I was told in particular that this used car was not only as good as it was the day it came off the factory line but, because of the tuning up and the alterations, it was even better; that this used car would be truly a car that I could purchase and use in order to get about, protect myself properly and move from one place to another. But I undertook to check the statements of the used car salesman. I discovered that if I had bought that car I would have bought a real lemon, just as the people of this country and the people in this parliament, if they buy this particular bill, will be buying a lemon also.
I was interested, too, to listen to the sham battle, as it were between the Leader of the Opposition and the Minister of Justice, and I expect it will be carried on by the subsequent speakers. I could not help but think back to the time when under the Liberal government there was an inquiry into the flour or milling industry, and that it was the Liberal government that suppressed that particular report and prevented the proper prosecution of that particular case in the courts. As a result of the McGregor report being

Combines Investigation Act hidden, secreted, and the statute law being violated by the Liberal government an illegal condition which had been carried on for many years escaped proper prosecution. I hope the same thing does not exist under the Conservative government; that it does not undertake to suppress particular reports and to keep information from the public about activities discovered as a result of inquiries and investigations under the act, or under the amended act, if it gets that far.
It is the intention of the C.C.F. to oppose and to fight the progress of this particular bill at every stage in its proceedings, on second reading and in the banking and commerce committee also, and in the committee of the whole house, if and when the bill gets back here, and to propose alterations and amendments which we think are necessary if the legislation is not adequately amended and changed to protect the interests of the consumers of this nation. Then, we intend to fight it all the way, morning, noon and night, on third reading also.
There is only one part of it that we endorse. I do not wish to infringe the rules by making reference to specific details, but only to do so in a general way. I refer to the last clause, clause 23, which extends until the end of December, 1961 the fact that this act shall not apply to fishermen along the west coast. Even that December, 1961 extension is hardly adequate, knowing the full impact it is apt to have upon the fishing industry.
We are unalterably opposed to what is in fact a series of proposed amendments which do not, as we see it, clarify the present act but seek to wreck it. One may ask why we should be opposed. It is a valid question. The consumers, the general public, the people of Canada, however you want to refer to them, are the ones affected to the greatest degree by anti-combines legislation. It is their interest and their welfare with which we should be primarily concerned.
The small businessman is really in the same class as the consumers, and I am differentiating between small and large businesses. It is true that these individuals are virtually helpless and defenceless against encroachment by large corporations. They are defenceless against any illicit or illegal practices by large corporations in the fields covered by anti-combines legislation generally, such as price fixing, allocation of markets, restriction of production or distribution and so on.
The only way that the consumer is able to gain any assistance and have any defence in his efforts to get a square deal is by legislation, a defence that guarantees by law

that he will be protected, that is enforced by law to ensure his protection. There is a modicum of protection in the act at the present time but the bill does nothing to increase the degree of protection. It does nothing to assist in promoting the welfare of the consuming public. In fact, it detracts therefrom.
There are two more or less general spheres covered by the bill, as indicated both by the Minister of Justice and the Leader of the Opposition. One is the field of combines and conspiracy related to restrictive trade practices and the other is the field of the small businessman and his activities. So far as the larger corporations of the nation are concerned I am sure that the bill is quite pleasing to them. By having sponsored these amendments, which I will deal with in detail later, I am sure the government party will find the welcome mat displayed on the doorstep of these large corporations. As a result of this bill I am sure the party to which the minister and the other members of the government belong will find there will be no difficulty in filling the treasury chest at campaign time.
The bill also allows the government to tell small businessmen, upon whom it depends for a great deal of its support, at election time how decent the government has been toward them. We have a paradoxical situation of the government trying to be everything to everybody at the same time but it is not carried out in fact when we analyse the details of the bill and see its effect. The minister said last night, as found at the bottom of the righthand column on page 4340 of Hansard, with reference to the study that had been made:
This study was carried out in conjunction with the advisers of my department and of the combines investigation branch, as well as with representatives of business and business organizations who lost no time in making representations to us.
You bet they did not lose any time in making representations to the minister. After all, he is their friend and this bill represents one of the rewards his friends are receiving as a result of past favours. There are elements in Canada, notably those who have been and are still engaged in illicit price fixing and restrictive trade practices, who know how benevolent this bill is. It is a fact that some of these corporations which have been prosecuted in the past for infractions of the act have wanted to write protective features into the legislation for their own benefit to the detriment of the benefit of the consumers and they could not have done any better than to secure the loopholes that are provided under subclause 2 of clause 32.

I think we are entitled to assess the effectiveness of the act as it has been administered up to now and, based on that, see whether or not that effectiveness has been increased or detracted from by the bill. I think almost every minister who at any time has proposed amendments to the combines legislation has stated that one of its purposes is to ensure that competition remains in effect to the fullest possible degree and that the benefits of such competition in a free enterprise society accrue to the consumer. The second design of the act, as has been indicated by each minister who has had the responsibility of dealing with the anti-combines legislation, is to protect the consumer. One of the theories of free enterprise that we hear lauded so much is that automatically there is competition, that free enterprise and competition go hand in hand. However, the mere fact that we have such legislation on the statute books would indicate that this is not so, for if competition were an inherent part of the free enterprise philosophy one would not need this sort of legislation to ensure that it is maintained and to prohibit certain non-competitive and discriminatory practices.
There are a number of penalties and remedies set out in the act with which I should like to deal briefly. I think we may say there are five in particular although there are also ancillary remedies and penalties. One is that the governor in council may remove or lower customs duties if it is found that this will help to bring about the benefits of competition. Second, the Exchequer Court of Canada, upon information from the attorney general and Minister of Justice, may declare as void any exclusive patent or trade mark rights and may direct that the products on which the patent was issued -may be produced in some other fashion by another concern. This is designed to bring about competition. Then there is provision for court orders of prohibition to bring about the dissolution of mergers and monopolies and there is also provision for fines and/or imprisonment.
So far as the customs duty provision is concerned, which is the prerogative of the governor in council, obviously it is designed to bring competition into play from sources outside Canada and thus bring about price reductions through firms outside Canada sending goods into Canada at lower prices than those charged by the group within Canada enjoying the protection. This provision has, of course, been completely ineffective because it has never been used. I took it from the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition-if I am wrong I will stand corrected-that he suggested this could be one of the alternative procedures to prosecution
Combines Investigation Act resulting in a fine or imprisonment, but everyone knows that when the Liberals were in office for so many years they never made use of this section of the act. Nevertheless, hindsight enlightenment is welcome and, as I have said on other occasions, it is amazing how stimulating defeat at the polls is upon the imagination and the development of new ideas.
The section of the act dealing with patent rights is also designed to allow the exchequer court to void those patents and to direct that the product may be produced by other companies. This provision is designed to bring competition into play within the country, but has never been used and that is why, in itself, it is not effective. The remarks I have made about the Liberals being in office and their lack of action in connection with customs duties also apply to the patent rights section because, as I say, it has never been used in any way.
I would point out here, and perhaps this is an aside but it is a related matter, that sometime ago I asked a question with respect to the issuance of patents for antibiotic drugs, the tetracycline group of so-called wonder drugs. In almost every case the patents in connection with these drugs have been issued to United States concerns, and I do not mean Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies but to the parent companies in the United States. Almost all of them were issued while the Liberal government was in office. We all know that the prices of the tetracycline group of drugs have remained static ever since 1951, regardless of the fact there has been an increase in production and regardless of the entry of new companies into the production of antibiotics. Surely there is a prima facie case here that these companies which have patents-true, they are outside of Canada but the patents were issued under our law -have been using these patent rights to unnecessarily hold up the prices for antibiotics. As I said, that is an aside.
Another remedy lies in the fact that the courts can issue an order for the prohibition of the continuation of an offence. I do not really see how this provision brings into play any degree of competition. It merely prevents the continuation of any particular offence. Later on I hope to explain how this order for the prohibition of the continuation of an offence can be effectively bypassed by any group of companies that wants to do so under the price leadership theory.
Then there is a provision for the dissolution of mergers which has not been used at all. I understand that there would have been such an application in the Canadian
4376	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act Breweries case if that case had proceeded along the lines hoped for by the crown in its attempt to prosecute. Quite frankly, I think they gave that case away, but that is another matter with which I shall deal later.
Then the fines and jail sentences are the penalties contained in this legislation. They do not bring competition into play, they merely penalize for past infractions. Incidentally, I do not believe they can be considered, perhaps to a slight degree, as deterrents to corporations that want to infringe the law in connection with these restrictive practices. For one thing, there has never been a jail sentence imposed, at least not to my memory, for an infraction of the section relating to a conspiracy to fix prices. I am quite sure that if some of the judges in this country had acted with that degree of perseverance with which they have acted in other cases and had imposed some jail sentences as a result of convictions under this section it would have been a more effective deterrent than it has been so far. However, no jail sentences have been imposed. If they had been, perhaps the price fixers would not have been able to operate so easily and so freely as they have.
Fines have been the major method of dealing with a conspiracy to fix prices. Practically all the prosecutions which have resulted in convictions have led to the imposition of fines. What, in reality, do these fines mean? I should like to explain why, in many cases, they are not an effective deterrent, if that is what they were designed to be. Certainly fines do not promote competition which is one of the ends to which this act is supposed to lead.
May I take just one isolated case, although there are others. In the farm fencing case a number of firms were fined for price fixing arrangements, and I should like to relate those figures to indicate just how little a fine means in some cases. This information was obtained as a result of a question I asked. The Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited was convicted and fined under, I believe it would be section 411 of the Criminal Code, for fixing the prices of farm fencing and link fencing. This corporation was fined $10,000 in 1956. Ten thousand dollars may seem like a pretty hefty fine for any one corporation or individual to pay, but in reality this amount was only three twentieths of one per cent of the net profit made by Dosco in 1956, or one cent for every $6 of net profit. I refer only to the year in which the fine was imposed, but if the fine were spread over the 20-year period of the conspiracy the amount would be even more infinitesimal.


The Steel Company of Canada was also fined $10,000. Stelco was in a bit better position because the fine meant only four one hundredths of one per cent of the net profit of Stelco in 1956, or one cent for every $25 of net profit in that particular year. There were a number of other corporations involved and my examination reveals that no fine ranged higher than 1.8 per cent of the net profit of the corporation for that particular year. In reality this is nothing more than a licence fee for engaging in these assorted practices, regardless of the fact that Stelco, Dosco and the other steel companies were engaged for a period of more than 20 years in milking the farmers of this country for every penny they could, and in milking the government of this country for every penny they could.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps some one of the cabinet ministers will at least read in Hansard what I am saying so that the suggestions I am about to make can be considered because I do not see any of them in the house at the moment.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: In relating the fine to the net profit in a given year for the company in question is the hon. member implying that the total net profit was of an illegal nature?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I did not imply that at all. I merely pointed out what these fines meant in relation to the net profit picture of these companies. There are other cases in that particular year in which fines were imposed. I was pointing this out to indicate that in effect these fines are nothing more than a licensing fee to operate illegally. I was saying that a fine of one cent for every $25 net profit means very little to a company like Stelco.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: If the hon. member wants to be fair, what he means is that the total operations of that company are illegal, not the particular operation which was exposed by the investigation.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is now making a statement. I assume he will have an opportunity to participate in the debate and he can make that statement if he so desires. The hon. member initially asked a question as to whether or not that was what I was saying and I said no that was not what I was saying. He can interpret it the other way if he so wishes, and say that every dollar Stelco gained that year was illegal; that is his business, not mine. What I was suggesting was that in relation to the question

of fines there should be an alteration in the approach to the employment of fines.
I would suggest that consideration be given to establishing a fine on a percentage basis, perhaps between 5 per cent and 20 per cent of the net profits of the company say over the past 10 years or for a lesser period of time if the illicit practice has been engaged in for that lesser period of time. This fine, with a minimum of 5 per cent, would establish a penalty which would act as a deterrent by the mere fact it was there. It would act as a deterrent because it is a potential fine. It would also to a degree recoup society by money going into the general revenue some of the money which that corporation had taken by illegal means over the years in which it had been engaged in these activities. It would also give discretion to the court, by placing a 5 per cent minimum and say a 20 per cent maximum, to operate within this area and to assess the degree of illegal activity and decide whether or not a greater or a lesser fine should be imposed.
If I may be permitted to do so, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could make some reference now to proposals to amend section 32, not in detail but in general, and point out that all of our convictions in the past have been based on and obtained as a result of having access to letters, documents, memoranda, minutes of meetings and so on which set out the desires of the companies to engage in certain price fixing arrangements. But what is occurring or what is developing is that these same organizations or new ones can engage in price fixing now without fear of being detected by the price leadership approach. This is generally as follows and I only set this out in general terms. Suppose there are six companies that want to engage in fixing prices. If one of them raises the price of its product on a particular day and its other five so-called competitors raised their prices on following days, within the next week or two, this is known as price leadership and it is impossible to prosecute; it is impossible to detect.
The minister made reference to the escape parts of clause 32 and that they were leaving in effect the definition of a combine and he made reference to price fixing. He made reference to certain co-operative activities which would be beneficial, I think he said, to society although perhaps he meant beneficial to a certain select private group. These cooperative activities are as follows. I only make general reference to them without reading because I realize that is contrary to the rules. Now a group of corporations-if this bill becomes law-can engage in a conspiracy to fix prices and can have as a defence that they were exchanging statistics. The statistics
Combines Investigation Act are price lists. But if there is an exchange of price lists and competitors follow suit within the next few days under the price leadership approach we have price fixing but it has been legalized by reference here to the exchange of statistics.
They can co-operate on the defining of production standards. They can give a detailed account to each of their so-called competitors about production standards and quality of the products they are producing and within a short while the same group of people can be engaged in price fixing or a production restriction program and engaged in price fixing by price leadership and it can even be completely authoritatively done. They can co-operate in research and development which would be a great boon to the drug industry which already co-operates in the use of research. If that is not sufficient, if the minister has not given enough loopholes and enough legislative authority to price leadership to take over, he throws in a catch-all phrase that they can engage in some other manner not enumerated.
I have only a moment or two left, Mr. Speaker, so I am not going beyond this point into the question of the small businessmen and the price allowances, discriminatory practices and so on. That matter will be dealt with later on by other speakers. But these amendments simply legalize the price leadership approach to price fixing, restricting production and carving up markets and give statutory and parliamentary blessing to abuses of this sort and to setting up private price control agencies which will from here on in be able to operate with immunity and without fear of detection or prosecution because regardless of the minister's comments and the misinformation he gave us about the beneficial effect this would have on society, it will have a decidedly detrimental effect on society. I would venture to say they will never have another prosecution or probably never take another case to court under section 32 for restrictive practices, conspiracy and combines with respect to any of the clauses (a), (b), (c) or Cd) of section 32 (1). This in itself will have an enhancing effect on the present trend toward business itself, something to which the minister made some slight reference. But he makes no reference in the bill as to what can be done to cope with the question of bigness and it is an important problem. This will be enhanced and gain will be made by those who want to engage in the same practices in which they have engaged previously at the expense of the consumer.
It is unfortunate that the minister did not set up this royal commission he talked about
4378	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act when he took office instead of consulting his friends who are not in the house even or who are not even within his own department in order to determine from them what alterations and what changes should be made.
As I mentioned, my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. But perhaps I shall have an opportunity at some other stage of the proceedings, such as at the committee stage, to put into words some of the thoughts I have on this particular bill. I am sure that other members of the C.C.F. will do so because, as I said, we intend to fight this bill morning, noon and night at every step of its progress. We will take the opportunity later on to discuss the dilatoriness, the detrimental effects of the other parts of the bill, the merger question, the question of monopolies, the question of the elimination by the back door of the resale price maintenance section and other factors of that nature.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are not many bills that come before parliament that draw a clear line of demarcation between the philosophy of the government party and that of the Liberal party. From time to time such a bill does come before the house and it is basically one that sets out the differences between the two parties. For example, a bill dealing with the question of high or low tariff protection is one that sometimes comes before the house and is one in which we recognize the lines of party differences. The present bill before the house reflects, in my judgment, that classical and traditional difference between the Conservative party and the Liberal party and their philosophies. Because the present bill falls into that class I think we should give it as close attention as possible and perhaps should be able to express opinions as to the two different philosophies.
This one, for example, clearly establishes in my judgment the clash between the classes, the industrial and commercial tycoons on the one hand and the consumer masses on the other hand. Because we are concerned with that philosophy which politics preaches, the greatest good for the greatest number, we feel that this classical difference establishes the point of view that the Liberal party holds, that any legislation which is going to show any preference to business and industry at the expense and to the prejudice of the large masses of the public across the country is legislation which we oppose, and, as my leader has said, oppose down the line because, as he so well and thoroughly illustrated, this is not a measure that would legislate the greatest good for the greatest number. As I said a moment ago, it is actually a clash between the control of big business over the freedom of competitive trade.


The historic position of the two parties was outlined by my leader with his customary precision and factual truth last night and once again he placed these two points of view into proper focus. As I listened to the minister I got the distinct impression that he was presenting a sort of apology for having to introduce this legislation, and I was reminded of the French proverb, "Qui s'excuse, s'accuse". In his presentation I found that he laboured. He did not appear to be convinced that he was philosophically right in what he was actually doing, because I believe that way down deep he must revolt at this type of legislation, which is commanded only by a loyalty to the philosophy of a party and not by personal conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is wrong as usual and also out of order.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister attempted to straddle in colossus-like proportions the classical gap between big business in the form of combines, trusts and cartels, and free and competitive trading. The fact is that this cannot be done. The government's majority will get the legislation on the statute books in all probability, but it will only do what former Conservative governments have done and that is to destroy an effective combines law which was sustained over and over again by the supreme court and indeed by the privy council, despite the frequent attempts by the Conservative party, in league with big business, to destroy it.
The minister was at great pains to repeat several times in a serious attempt to impress the house that this was not a revision of the act but was only an amendment. I noted that he repeated that statement more than once. Well, Mr. Speaker, he may call it an amendment-and technically he is perfectly right, it is an amending bill-but the amendment attempts to remove whole sections, important sections, and replace them with others which alter the basic purpose of the act. The act is left with the introductory clause and with other sections in the act which are meaningless but are necessary to give it form. But certainly the amending bill, because it introduces so many new sections and removes the basic sections of the act, could in every sense with the exception of the technical meaning one can give to it, be a revision of the act now existing.
I say that instead of tightening up loopholes of escape for big business offenders, the minister not only widens these loopholes but creates new ones which will be pointed out when we examine the bill section by section in committee. Under the rules we cannot do that at the present time, but I

hope when it comes before the banking and commerce committee and in committee of the house after second reading we will be able to indicate that more avenues of escape have been created than should have been prevented. As a matter of fact, as I see it the minister is attempting to perform and probably will be successful in performing a very dexterous dental operation. He is really extracting the teeth from the act, and as I said before will probably prove himself to be a very successful dental surgeon.
I have the feeling that if the government did not fear great public resentment they would in all probability repeal the entire act as it now exists.

NORTHERN PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-31, an act to incorporate Northern Pipe Line Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is for the purpose of incorporating Northern Pipe Line Company into a dominion company with head office at Regina in Saskatchewan. The purpose of the act is to create a company to apply to the national energy board for a permit or permits to construct, own and operate pipe lines for the transmission and transportation of gas, oil and other liquid hydrocarbons within and outside of Canada.
It is expected that the company will have Canadian and United States shareholders of financial and business responsibility as and when it is ready to proceed with a program for financing and constructing pipe line facilities. In the meantime the principal beneficial shareholder is Minnesota Pipe Line Company, a corporation organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the state of Delaware with its principal office located at Saint Paul, Minnesota. The extent of the interest of the Minnesota Pipe Line Company in this new company, Northern Pipe Line Company, when the plan of organization is complete, has not been determined and will remain an open question until such time as the Northern Pipe Line Company is ready to proceed with its application to the national energy board.
The chief beneficial owner, Minnesota Pipe Line Company, owns and operates a 16-inch crude oil pipe line system extending from a take-off point on the interprovincial pipe line system at Clearbrook, Minnesota, a distance of 256 miles. The Minnesota pipe line system is transporting about 40,000 barrels a day of Canadian crude oil to United States' markets. That pipe line system originally cost about $12,800,000. Its replacement cost as of today would be about $16 million.
As and when Northern Pipe Line Company has been incorporated by act of parliament it is contemplated that an application will be made to the national energy board for a permit to construct a 16-inch or larger crude oil pipe line system near Regina, Saskatchewan, to a point on the international boundary

Private Bills
line between Canada and the United States near North Portal, Saskatchewan, a distance of about 153 miles. An estimate of the cost of this crude oil pipe line system is $10,500,000.
It is contemplated that the Northern Pipe Line Company would connect with and deliver crude oil and other liquid hydrocarbons to a 16-inch or larger crude oil pipe line system to be constructed from a point near Portal, North Dakota, to connect with the Minnesota pipe line system at Clearbrook, Minnesota, a distance of about 330 miles.
The Northern pipe line system would transport and deliver to the United States pipe line system in the initial stages approximately 26,000 barrels a day of Fosterton type crude oil now being transported by the south Saskatchewan pipe line system from the Fosterton, Dollard and other fields in southwest Saskatchewan via Regina and initially approximately 12,000 barrels a day of the Midale type crude and other types of crude oil now being or to be produced in the fields of southeast Saskatchewan. It is contemplated that the United States pipe line system would transport initially about 20,000 barrels a day of crude oil from fields in the Williston basin area in North Dakota for delivery into the Minnesota pipe line system.
This proposed Northern pipe line system is required to provide more economical transportation for Canadian crude oils to United States' markets and to expand markets for Canadian crude oil.
I might add that as at December, 1954 there were 1,094 oil wells in Saskatchewan. As at December, 1956 the number had increased to 2,414. As at December, 1954 there were 30 oil fields in Saskatchewan and as at December, 1956 this number had increased to 46. In 1956 over $600 million was spent in western Canada on exploration and oil field development programs. Saskatchewan is the second greatest oil producing province in Canada. The establishment of this company will mean employment in Saskatchewan and a financial investment in that province as well as a market for our crude oil.
The persons who are interested in incorporating this company are already interested in Saskatchewan oil. They drilled the discovery well in the Fosterton field in the southeast corner of the Kindersley constituency approximately 35 or 40 miles northwest of Swift Current. They also have other interests in addition to their interest in the Fosterton field.
If the bill receives second reading I intend to move that it be referred to a standing committee of this house where all details can be discussed and witnesses appear to answer all questions that may be put with regard

to the incorporation of the company, the shareholders, the financial setup, etc. As I have already stated, before any construction will be proceeded with it will be necessary for the company to make application to the national energy board for its approval. I move the second reading of this bill, seconded by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Ormis-ton), and commend it to the favourable consideration of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for the explanation he has given the house about the reasons for the company seeking incorporation by special act and the explanation he has given as to the intentions of the company after incorporation.
I wish to raise one other matter. I regret that in his remarks the hon. gentleman did not deal with the matter of the urgency of bringing this bill forward out of its regular place on the order paper. What it means is an added difficulty in bringing the session to a conclusion because all hon. members will have to remain in the chamber of the House of Commons at all times and can no longer rely on the order paper for the sequence of business. That is, unanimous consent for bringing forward business out of its regular sequence as indicated on the order paper can be obtained at any moment in the proceedings without any explanation whatever for that being given to hon. members.
I believe the house is entitled to know in advance, if possible, what the order of business will be although I appreciate that in some cases it is not possible. Surely some reason for this practice is owed to other hon. members who are interested in legislation. They are entitled to know the reason for the urgency in dealing with this matter ahead of the several hundred other private bills that are on the order paper ahead of it.
However, be that as it may, I have no criticism whatever of the hon. member on that score because I know it was not any wilful omission on his part in any way. My purpose is rather to draw the attention of the house to that practice which in my opinion is dangerous to the rights of debate and to the rights of hon. members of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: NORTHERN PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Would the hon. gentleman make it clear that this is not government legislation?

maintopic: NORTHERN PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Oh, quite. I want to make it entirely clear that this is a private bill. I was not criticizing the government for it at all. I was merely attempting to draw attention to a practice that is growing up in the private members' hour that can be harmful to the conduct of business in the house.

There is another matter which I feel I should raise at an early stage in the discussion of the bill although I do not know whether it would be more properly raised on second reading or in committee. Perhaps it should be mentioned now so there will be notice of it at the earliest possible moment. I refer to the name of the company. We have an application for incorporation of a company under the name of Northern Pipe Line Company. At the same time we have in existence and operating through a wide area of Canada a pipe line company incorporated by special act of parliament and called Trans-Northern Pipe Line Company. We also have a crown corporation known as Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. It seems to me that to grant a name so similar to that of two operating companies already in existence, without some explanation as to the reason for the name, or some other explanation as to why that name should be granted to this company, is setting a dangerous precedent. I have asserted on other occasions, on other bills the proposition that there is likely to be confusion by the public of the names by reason of the names granted to companies incorporated by special acts of parliament.
There is no procedure in parliament for examining the possibility of confusion in the names being granted as there is in letters patent companies, and this particular name sought by those incorporators raises that very question in a very precise way. I hope that at the committee stage consideration can be given to the question as to whether or not, in the opinion of the committee and later when the bill is returned to the house, in the opinion of the house, there is likely to be confusion caused to the public by the granting of this amendment.
There is nothing more for me to say about the substance of the bill because facts having to do with the company itself can be brought out at the committee stage and can be dealt with more appropriately there.

Although there are four children the husband in his answers indicated that he is 35 years old; that he lives at St. Sophie, in Terrebonne county, province of Quebec. Questioning by the clerk brings out the following information:
Q. At the time the petition was drafted, where were you living?
A. At 462 Ouimet street, in St. Jerome.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Labourer.
Q. Are you married and if so to whom?
A. Yes, to Aurore Belanger.
Q. When were you married?
A. August 23, 1947.
Q. Where were you married?
A. In St. Therese de Blainville, Terrebonne county, province of Quebec.
Q. By whom?
A. By l'Abbe Vezeau.
Q. What is your religion?
A. I was a Catholic at the time.
Q. And what religion was your wife?
A. She was a Catholic also.
Q. I show you a document. Do you recognize it?
A. That is my marriage certificate.
At that point, it is very interesting to note that, in keeping with something that I was told not long ago by one of the learned lawyers, there is no divorce possible for Catholic people. He pointed out that as a Catholic himself he had no objection to acting in divorce cases for the simple reason that no Catholic could obtain a divorce. He said that if they took this procedure they were not Roman
[The Deputy Chairman.]
Catholics. Therefore it is interesting to note in the evidence that the petitioner said:
A. I was a Catholic at the time.
Q. And what religion was your wife?
A. She was a Catholic also.
He agrees that the information in the marriage certificate filed as exhibit No. 1 is correct and also that exhibit No. 2, the photograph, is a close likeness of his wife and that the photograph is only a couple of years old. The lawyer in this case was Alvin B. Jacobs from the city of Montreal. He appeared for the petitioner and he asked the following questions:
Q. Where were you born?
A. At St. Scholastique, in the county of Two Mountains, province of Quebec.
Q. Have you always resided in the province of Quebec?
A. Yes.
Q. During your marriage with your wife where did you live?
A. In Ste. Therese and St. Jerome.
Q. Did you have any children with your wife?
A. Yes, four.
Q. Can you give their names and how old they
are?
A. Louise, born July 28, 1948; Yves, born December 18, 1950; Daniel, born November 8, 1952; Denis, born January 23, 1955.
Q. With whom are the children living today?
A. They are with me.
Q. How did you get along with your wife during the time you lived together?
A. Not very well.
I think that some comment is called for there. It would appear that they got along fairly well at particular times and that the situation here did not involve aggravation built up over a period of time. Something must have happened in this particular case. I think this is also in keeping with what learned counsel indicated to me the other day, that in the majority of bona fide cases there are other circumstances than the charge of adultery in a motel or some place else that is put forward for our benefit. It is not the actual cause of the dissolution of the marriage. I see one learned hon. member listening. This gentleman pointed out that he had handled 10 cases and that in 9 of them detectives were not used as the evidence was quite easily obtainable in other ways. This man lived with his wife over some period of years and therefore when he answered "not very well" to the question as to how he got along with his wife I think that was stretching the point considerably.
It reminds one of the old story of the man and woman who were visited by a gentleman and he observed that they did not talk to each other. He asked them if this had been going on for a long time and he was told that they had not talked to each other for years. Then he noticed a number of little children and he asked whose children they were. He was told they were theirs. He said,

"But you have not talked to your wife for years" and the answer was, "We do not get along that badly". So perhaps the answer "not very well" does not mean exactly what it says. Then the petitioner was asked these questions:
Q. What trouble did you have?
A. My wile was going out a lot and she was using bad language to the children, she was blaspheming. Often, while the three oldest ones were to school she would have the baby minded by a neighbour and she would go out in the afternoon.
Q. Now, did you live intimately as man and wife with your wife all the time?
A. No. About a year and a half or two years before the date of November 24 my wife did not want to sleep with me any longer.
Q. Do you personally know what happened on November 24, 1958 between your wife and Paul Emile Labelle?
A. Yes.

A. Yes.

I think hon. members should be very interested in that question.
A. After the detectives obtained the key to the motel and they walked in-

I suggest that the lawyer in this case asked the type of questions which would tend to obtain the answers that he wished. In the case before us we learn from the evidence that this man was an unemployed carpenter. He makes less than $85 a week and he is only employed on a seasonal basis. He has four children and he has to live in somebody else's house. He has to have people look after his children.
I suggest that this man does not necessarily want to get married. He is not earning enough to keep his family and there is no apparent reason why he should be obtaining a divorce at all. I think if he were given his way this particular case would have meant the end of this relationship but there would have been no hurry to get this divorce. I also suggest, and it should have been quite obvious to the legal counsel who was asking these questions; I suggest it was, and he did not ask certain questions because that would have defeated his purpose-that the person who wants the divorce is the woman in this

particular case. Likely arrangements have been made with this Paul Emile Labelle, and she wants to marry him. It is true that in the petition there is no mention of them, but the other place did give some consideration to their welfare. However, I do not intend to refer


to that. Senator Roebuck, the chairman of the committee, asked these questions:
Q. Have you got a job?
A. No, not at present. I worked as a carpenter this summer but it is seasonal work and I am not employed at the moment.
Q. How much do you make?
A. Two dollars an hour and more.
Q. Is that sufficient to keep your family?
A. Yes.
Q. Will you likely be going to work again shortly?
A. Yes.
Q. How many hours a day do you work?
A. About 10 hours, it depends where.
Q. Would it be usually $20 a day you make when you are working?

maintopic: ROGER VERMETTE
speechtext: What are you talking about now, unemployment?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ROGER VERMETTE
speechtext: No, I am just indicating that this man only earns this amount of money. I am suggesting that he cannot pay for this divorce. I have not seen any evidence indicating any reason why he should obtain this divorce. I am suggesting, therefore, that the divorce is not being paid for by the petitioner but is very likely being paid for by the corespondent. There should have been more questions directed to this matter because, as the evidence indicates, the amount he has earned has not been enough for him to keep his family.

Somebody says it is relevant, and I think it is relevant. If the hon. member had said "irrelevant", I would not have been so sure. I think it does matter. This man earns $90 a week but is only employed seasonally. He probably does not work more than half the year.
Senator Roebuck asked these questions:
Q. Do you own any property?
A. No.
Q. Do you own your own house?
A. No.
Q. Have you got any money in the bank?
A. Not much.
Q. Do you own any stocks or bonds?
A. No.
Then Mr. Jacobs makes a statement about the man's financial situation. This probably proves exactly what I am saying. The lawyer, knowing full well how much it costs to get a divorce through parliament, makes the claim that this man has not earned enough money to pay for it and, therefore, he should be given back some of the money paid in fees. He says:
Mr. Chairman, I would make application that under the circumstances of this man's financial situation and particularly in view of the fact that there are four young children to bring up, that part of the parliamentary fee be remitted to him. As to the amount, I would leave it to the discretion of the committee.

It should be borne in mind that the parliamentary fee is only $210 but that a divorce costs, on the average, $2,500. It seems to me that the lawyer is just trying to make it look good for himself and at the same time get some consideration for the man. I am very pleased to say that the committee did give consideration to this application and agreed to reduce the fee to $100, giving the man back $110.
The investigators in this case are old friends of this committee. They have been here on numerous cases. They always give the same type of evidence. Having read all the evidence in this particular case, I think you will be pleasantly surprised to know that there is a change in the evidence. This time they had no clothes on. Before they always wore baby doll pyjamas or something like that.
Then, Gerard Daigneault, 32, of Montreal, gives his evidence.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Investigator.
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. I show you a photograph which has been filed as Exhibit 2, can you identify the woman in it?
A. That is Mrs. Roger Vermette.
Q. Did you have occasion to conduct an investigation into the conduct of Mrs. Roger Vermette?
A. I did, sir.
Q. Over what period of time?
A. Our services being retained by you, Mr. Jacobs, during the first week of November, 1958, at which time you furnished us with this photograph over here and also giving us certain information, I started investigation with Mr. Paquette, and as a result of that investigation on November 24, 1958, accompanied by Mr. Vermette and Mr. Paquette, at approximately 8.30 p.m., at the Moulin Rouge motel, near St. Jean, in Quebec, unit 15 after having obtained the pass key from the proprietor of the hotel the three of us proceeded to unit 15.
I have seen this motel. It is a very pretty place. It is a large, elaborate motel. I think if the corespondent can take his girl friend there he can well afford to pay for this divorce and he should get no sympathy from us. But to anybody who wishes to stay at a motel I would suggest that if detectives float around with a whole pocketful of keys it might not be the best place in the world to spend a week end. The questioning continues:
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. Who were the three?
A. Mr. Paquette, Mr. Vermette, and myself. After opening the door with the aid of the pass key I put on the ceiling light to the right as you entered-
You see, Mr. Chairman, if this were even an hotel, from my reading of detective stories and that sort of thing, normally even if they were police they would not let people go into it themselves. The manager or the detective of the hotel or the desk clerk or somebody would go up with the pass key and

would open the door. Instead of there being three there, there would have been four because the hotel official would very likely have been along. I see no reason why he should entrust the pass key which can be duplicated for any room in the hotel very simply or why he should give it to some other party. But things are done differently in Quebec than they are done elsewhere. That may be the answer. Anyway the evidence continues as follows:
After opening the door with the aid of the pass key I put on the ceiling light to the right as you entered and there right in front of us both Mrs. Vermette and the man who was with her were completely naked on the bed. As we entered the woman shouted, "Paul", and she took the white covers and covered herself up with the covers. Then I went to her, and she was holding the covers over her face like that, and I took her hand away and I asked Mr. Vermette, "Is that your wife?" He said yes. Then he added, "This is where you go for your moving picture." And I then asked the man's name; first he refused, and then I told him I would know just the same because his car was at the door. Then he wanted me to identify myself properly, which I did, and then I asked him for his car registration: he gave me his car registration and on it was written "Paul Emile Labelle", address 20-72nd avenue. St. Therese, Quebec. I asked him if that was his real name, and he said yes. After telling the both of them they would be hearing from Mrs. Vermette's attorney we left the premises.
Mr. Chairman, in a case we had the other day I mentioned the fact that quite often this question is put and this is one of those cases in which it is put:
I asked him if that was his real name, and he said yes.
This is the only case I have noted for some time where this question has been asked. I think it is a procedure that the other place would be wise to insist on. If they did so, probably some remarkable and surprising things might be prevented, if television stories give an indication of what may happen in this type of case. The questions continue:
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. How many beds were in the room?
A. Only one bed.
Q. You stated they were both lying there naked; what were they doing?
A. Well, actually I think they were looking at T.V.
Q. And after that did you and Mr. Paquette drive Mr. Vermette home?
A. We did, sir. When they registered it was 6.45 p.m. and I left Mr. Paquette there and I went and got Mr. Vermette at his home at St. Jerome.
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. Did you see any clothes around the premises?
A. Yes, a woman's clothing, underwear, were on the bench at the foot of the bed. The other thing, the two of them were not lying with their heads at the head of the bed, the two of them had their heads at the foot of the bed.

Mr. Chairman, it surprises me that this should constitute adultery. We know that there are many people in Canada who run around with their clothes off quite a bit of the time in nudist camps, when the weather is warm enough; and I have heard that they are as moral places as there are in existence. It may be quite natural to run around disrobed in that circumstance. It may be very comfortable to run around in motels with no clothes on and to watch television. petition and by subsequent evidence? Perhaps this is a reason why the members of the other place raise questions with respect to the children. I do not know whether you would like to deal with that question right at the moment or at some later date, Mr. Chairman.

That your petitioner has ascertained that the respondent, Aurore Belanger, committed adultery on November 24, 1958, in the town of St. Janvier, in the district of Terrebonne, at the Moulin Rouge motel unit 15, with Paul Emile Labelle, who resides at 20-72nd avenue, St. Therese, Quebec.

If this chamber's decision is that adultery has been proven by this particular bill, then I suggest we have a new definition in Canada of adultery.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment of the debate at five o'clock I was talking about the various attitudes that the government party and the official opposition adopted in the past in dealing with the subject of and legislating upon combines, the Combines Investigation Act, mergers and trusts. I stated that there were divergent views, each party treating these questions in accordance with their political philosophy and thinking.
In this connection may I point out that so long as Sir Robert Borden was in power there were no anti-combines investigations at all. There were no prosecutions despite the fact that there was an effective law on the statute books. The Conservative philosophy in this regard throughout the years and especially in the period between 1910 and 1937 was, interestingly enough, revealed by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, a former Conservative leader, when speaking in the other place and when as reported at page 525 of the Senate Hansard, he used these words:
We struggled so much to legitimize combines that we exceeded the constitution.
That is a frank and honest statement by a responsible and reputable leader who did not hesitate to express his point of view. In colloquial language I would say that the hon. gentleman certainly pulled no punches in expressing his views and those of the Conservative party in relation to combines.
A perfect illustration of the Conservative party's desire to protect combines over the years is to be found in a piece of legislation enacted by the Bennett government in 1935. A clause was introduced into that legislation by the government of the day which virtually made the existing anti-combines laws impotent. This is how it was done. The clause provided that all the evidence acquired in an investigation as to whether a combine existed or did not exist and all the information and material accumulated by the investigators were inadmissible in an open court. That was the effect of the provision. I submit that no combine could be successfully prosecuted without the evidence obtained for the director by the investigators to enable him to decide whether or not there should be a prosecution.
Perhaps the house would permit me to give an analogy. Assume that our security police were on the trail of a spy or a spy ring following a major crime and had accumulated information and evidence on which a prosecution could be based. How frustrating it would be if they found there was a law which
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rae).]

prohibited the production in court of all the evidence and material acquired in the course of their investigation. That was the effect of the amendments to the legislation in 1935. This ingenious pro-combine enactment by the Bennett government was later declared ultra vires by the courts and sanity and effectiveness were again restored to the Combines Investigation Act by the Liberal government.
I was not impressed by the undue concern which the minister in his remarks expressed for the small storekeeper when he said that we should protect the maximum number of small storekeepers. Of course we should. No one would disagree with that statement. I should like to point out to the minister and the house that this was only one of the ways by which the minister sought to justify resale price maintenance. In this way the minister directly helps stifle free and competitive trade. That is certainly not beneficial to the great buying public. To do so would be to enact a law that would not provide the maximum good for the maximum number. I see it only as a form of crocodile tears which the minister sheds for the small storekeepers. It is nothing less than an indirect way of helping maintain prices dictated by manufacturers. The small storekeeper has not the means of meeting competition. He must obtain his merchandise from the manufacturer. He is the one who will be compelled to maintain the prices that are fixed and dictated by the manufacturer.
I wish now to say a few words about some of the escape clauses in the bill. While not referring to any particular clause I wish to address myself to those escape clauses which provide a good defence to a prosecution. In a new provision in the bill an escape or a good defence against the prosecution is possible if the combine exists for the purpose of (a) an exchange of statistics, (b) defining product standards, (c) an exchange of credit information, (d) definition of trade terms, (e) cooperation in research and development, (f) restriction of advertising, and (g) some other matter not enumerated in subsection (3). Surely (g) is a very peculiar provision. This is the first time that I have ever encountered such a clause that outlines the things that provide a proper defence to a prosecution. There is also some other matter not enumerated in subsection (3). I should like to ask the minister where he has seen a clause of a similar nature? Can the minister tell the house what the clause refers to when it speaks of a probable defence for some other matter which is not enumerated in subsection (3>? I would be interested in hearing from the minister if he would care to answer the question
now.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you very much. Once we realize that there are six or seven means by which industry can form a combine- and certainly they run the whole gamut there -I put this question to the house: What else, short of an open agreement on prices, can there be to make such a complete combine? That seems to me to be the only thing that was omitted. All these things which the combine is permitted to do certainly will produce profit for the members of the combine. Certainly, more efficiency, reduction of cost of operation, will certainly create more profits and, of course, we all know that there is no altruism in business, especially in big business. Altruism in business would clash with big dividends, and I am sure the minister does not think that parliament is so naive as to think otherwise. This whole new clause- and it is a completely new section-clearly permits the establishment of a combine and peculiarly enough a closed combine, because the clause does not state that everyone in that particular business or industry can have membership in the combine or can enjoy the benefit of this joint activity. Will they at any time be compelled to take in new members, or does everyone in the industry have a right by law to be accepted in the combine so that they may benefit from all those economies which the minister states the combine can perform?
As I see it, those economies can be enjoyed only by members of the combine. All others in that same industry will be prejudiced by not having the benefits that their competitors have. There is no such section in the law, as I see it, that makes membership in such a combine available to everyone in that industry or, assuming that the combine has been created and new people come into the industry, who take up location and establish a similar industry, that they will be able to enjoy the benefits which their competitors enjoy unless the bill contains a clause which will keep such a combine open to everyone in the industry or compel it to accept new members. I say that the absence of such a section in the law would create an unfair situation and to some extent sanction illegal combines.
There are other clauses in the bill which provide other types of escape clauses. I refer to new clauses, although I do not name them by number. There is, for example, a new term that I see for the first time. It speaks of substantially lessening competition. Apparently, it is permissible to lessen competition. Certainly that is an invasion of the combines investigation laws. Apparently
Combines Investigation Act competition can be lessened but that by itself is not an offence. We find that it becomes an offence when competition has been substantially lessened. By whom, and how will "substantially" be interpreted.

Then, Mr. Speaker, we have in the section the words "materially misleading''. This, as I say, is a new term. I do not know whether the minister will find a spot where it existed before and thereby seek to justify it on that ground rather than on the ground of good, sound law. It is permissible to mislead, apparently, but it is not permissible to materially mislead. When will misleading be material, or when will it not be material, and who will decide that? I mention these facts merely to emphasize that these amendments are being made not for the purpose of enlightening, explaining or assisting to understand the law but for the purpose of confusing it.
There is also a section which uses the language, "an inference unfavourable to the accused." Who or what will make it an inference? Who will decide that? Who will judge whether it is an inference and who will judge whether it is an inference and who makes it unfavourable? This is merely another provision which, while I do not say it was intentionally inserted in the bill for this purpose, certainly does not help to enlighten but rather confuses.
The words "reasonably expect" are also used, and in the context of the provision this is merely an attempt to read another person's mind.

defence. It would seem that a defence is possible when the breach of the act is for purposes which may be considered commendable. The question is, commendable to whom? The public Is entitled to the benefit of free competition, and the prohibitions of the act cannot be evaded by good motives. Whether they be innocent and even commendable, they cannot alter the true character of the combine which the law forbids, and the wish to accomplish desirable purposes constitutes no defence and will not condone the undue restraint, which is the elimination of the free domestic market.
