speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was slow in rising because I thought our friends opposite would have something to reply to what has been said up to now, but in view of the situation, I shall take part in the debate immediately instead of waiting until later on.
May I say at this early point that the resolution introduced by the Minister of Justice
Combines Investigation Act (Mr. Fulton), to amend the Combines Investigation Act, is certainly not a model of clarity.
What principle underlies this ambiguity? The purpose of the bill does not seem to be to protect the consumer or the corner grocery.
Last night the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) pointed out to the minister that he had all but forgotten to mention the protection that should be given to the consumer.
Instantly the minister jumped to his feet to say that the Leader of the Opposition had not listened too well to what he had been saying.
I made an effort today to read the speech through-this was no slight task either-and I have noted that the minister makes only two references to the consumer.
The following sentence is to be found on page 4348 of Hansard:
The first is how to get at this situation and find an effective method of dealing with it without doing the consumer ... a disservice ...
The second reference appears in the second column of the same page:
-practices which confer no lasting benefit on the consumer.
In his whole speech, which lasted an hour and a half, the minister managed to devote only two sentences to the consumer. Yet, if there is one group that is entitled to some protection, it is surely the consumer, even more than the dealer. It is generally the consumer who suffers when a piece of poor legislation is passed. It is not generally the dealer.
The first part of this bill, which is said to deal with monopolies, combines and mergers, apparently does not fulfil its purpose, because it opens up new possibilities to profiteers. I must point out, incidentally, that the validity of our legislation was always maintained whenever it came up before the supreme court.
On the other hand, looking at the second part of this bill, the part which deals particularly with misleading advertising and price fixing, we find that the Conservative party has come back in a round-about way to the minister's pet ideas.
I think the lack of clarity is intentional, because I would not do the Minister of Justice the affront of saying he has a confused mind.
In fact, despite its outward look of uprightness it does raise some typically Conservative dangers, of which we have been aware all along.

Combines Investigation Act
I realize this bill will be welcome by some people, those who will feel more at ease in their underhand practices to increase their profits, without any risk of being involved in a criminal offence under the law.
These amendments, in fact, are in line with the policy and philosophy of the Conservative party. Apparently, those hon. gentleman think that in order to ensure a permanent prosperity, you have to start from the top, that is, first see that the manufacturer, and the big businessman are prosperous, and when those people or corporations have accumulated enough pelf, they will let their surplus drop like a gentle rain upon the people at large.
You will allow me to have my doubts about it all, Mr. Speaker. When those people accumulate, they always find scores of ways of ploughing back their surplus into company expansion, so that it takes quite some time before the surplus reaches the masses. This bill was conceived with a similar purpose, that is, protection of the big, the strong, the powerful in the country; the others do not matter.
Mr. Speaker, like the press and various people in this country I was surprised by one thing: I mean the reason for which the Minister of Justice did not again introduce the bill he submitted to the house last year. Oh, he will probably tell me that, in the light of representations made to him, he thought it his duty to amend it. If the minister wants to change laws every time representations are made by certain groups, he will never see the end of it, and all our statutes will have to be revised. The minister should know by now that you can't please everybody.
The act which is now in force has always operated well, and each time a judgment has been rendered by a provincial court, indicting a corporation or a group of individuals, the supreme court has always upheld it. Therefore, if things have gone well, following careful inquiries made by the commission, and if the government has succeeded in securing convictions against operators of combines, I wonder for what particular reason, other than those outlined by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, this act should be amended. As I said earlier, I think it is only a reversion to the principles of the Conservatives who, in the past, have been accusing us of unfair interference in the commercial field. Besides, the Minister of Justice said yesterday that it was as a

result of public pressure, in 1889, that the first combines act was adopted. It was an amendment to the Criminal Code, into which section 498, now section 411, was inserted. It was really not anti-combine legislation; it was simply a section of the Criminal Code which made it possible, if necessary, to condemn those who went too far. But there was no organization which would provide for research, studies, and inquiries the result of which would be submitted to the court. As a matter of fact ten cases occurred between 1889 and 1900, and six were dismissed. That is to say that the legislation was not clear; that it was vague and had a few flaws. Later on, in 1900, under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, parliament amended the legislation by eliminating the word "illegally", which seems to have caused all the trouble. But when Mr. Mackenzie King, an outstanding economist, entered the Laurier cabinet as minister of labour, he worked out a bill on combines which seemed to cover everything and established the position somewhat better, so that inquiries could be carried out, that a commission could be responsible for their carrying out, in order to go to the root of the evil and to facilitate the good operation of that commission. That act, clear and specific, was enacted to protect both the small merchants and the public against operators of combines. Following the adoption of that act, price competition was recognized in a specific way. The Liberal party has always believed that fair competition should not be curtailed; it has always tried vigorously and successfully to supervise the operations of combines already in existence or in the process of organization, and it has always been through our courts that the law has been enforced. If, at times, discretionary powers were conferred upon ministers, those powers were merely complimentary, and did not replace the courts.
Mr. Speaker, we are not surprised at the present intervention. Every time the Conservative party came into power, it attempted by means of formulas that were sometimes very clever, to ease the application of the Combines Investigation Act introduced by the Liberal party.
The amendment now under consideration, if the minister sees fit to make use of it, might favour big companies, and goodness knows they do not need help from anyone. They are powerful enough.
We, Liberals, are proud of this act which led to the detection, prosecution and conviction of those who conspired at the expense of small businessmen.

From 1925 to 1957, 35 companies were prosecuted and convicted for breach of the Combines Investigation Act; they paid fines exceeding $1,600,000. Moreover, in 1957, when the Conservatives came into power, 21 cases were still under review. We have not heard much about them since then.
Mr. Speaker, I said that every time the Conservatives came into power they tried to do away with the combines act by making it inoperative.
From 1911 to 1921, during the term of Sir Robert Borden who, in 1910, had criticized and ridiculed the bill submitted by Mr. Mackenzie King, contending that it was uncalled-for interference in the field of business, no case was tried under the combines act. Sir Robert Borden was against the act, and would not enforce it. Anything went in those days of easy-does-it policy. And the Minister of Justice remarked yesterday: "We are thus abiding by the policy which was always followed by the Conservatives".
The minister also stated that the Conservatives had been accused of opposing the combines act and that this was untrue; he said the Conservatives had always been in favour of a combines act that was fair and could achieve its purpose. And yet, Sir Robert Borden, a Conservative leader whom the present Minister of Justice could not support, being too young, but whom his father has certainly supported, has expressed his opposition to the combines act, not only by ignoring it for nine years, but also by omitting any reference to it in his speeches.
In 1919, Sir Robert Borden's successor, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, set aside the combines act to replace it by two acts, that is, the Board of Commerce Act, and the Fair Prices Acts.
Those bills were intended to set up a federal board empowered-please note the spirit-to sanction price fixing. In short, it was supervising combines, not eliminating them. Besides, those two acts have been ruled ultra vires by our courts of justice, therefore unconstitutional.
And you will see Mr. Speaker, that a little later, Sir Robert Borden complained bitterly about it.
Following the return to power of the Liberals in 1923, a new combines bill was placed on the order paper. The improved bill was introduced by Mackenzie King against heavy
Combines Investigation Act opposition from the Conservatives, who said the bill represented unjustified and unwarranted interference in the field of business.
You will recognize, Mr. Speaker, that it took much more courage to introduce such a bill in 1923 than it does today for the Minister of Justice to submit his amendments, because in 1923, the Liberals had no absolute majority in parliament, whereas today, the Minister of Justice can rely on a heavy and servile majority.
In 1925, the 1923 legislation passed its first legal test with flying colours.
In 1930, after the Conservatives had been elected to office, the act again came under attack. Mr. Bennett, then prime minister, refused to publish reports submitted by Mr. Fred McGregor, registrar of the combines act. And the Minister of Justice said yesterday that he was following the same policy as the Conservatives have always followed.
Furthermore, every facility was then refused the McGregor commission, in order to hamper its work. No action was taken, despite the unpublished reports to the effect that the public was being victimized by the illegal and unfair practices of some companies.
If that is the minister's so-called effort to abide by the combines act and Conservative policy, well let him go right ahead and let the voting public be his judge in due course.
In 1935 the Bennett government passed legislation aimed at demolishing the combines act by placing the whole of it under the control of Mr. George Sedgwick, president of the tariff board, and that was another piece of Conservative legislation which was ruled ultra vires by the courts.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that each time the Conservatives introduce a bill- there is no doubt they have brilliant lawyers among them-they always introduce it in such a way that the courts will reject it, so they can say later: "It is not our fault; blame the courts." Well, if the bill they introduced had been well planned, I am sure that the courts would have maintained it just as they maintained the anti-combines acts adopted by the Liberal party.
After the Liberals returned to power in 1936, they rebuilt, under the leadership of Mr. Mackenzie King, an anti-combines act that stood the test of time to the general satisfaction. But, in that year, the act was not

Combines Investigation Act accepted by the Senate. In fact, the Senate, with a Conservative majority, did not let the bill go through. It was then that our friend, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, former prime minister of Canada and Conservative leader, said-an assertion nobody denied-in explanation of the opposition he was leading in the Senate against the combines act, as found at page 525 of the English text of the Senate Hansard of 1936:
We...
And this word "We" meant the Conservatives:
(Text):
We struggled so much to legitimize combines that we exceeded the constitution.
(Translation):
That was a statement made by a former leader of the Conservative party, a former prime minister, who said: "We struggled so much to legitimize combines that we exceeded the constitution".
Is that what the minister means when he says he will follow the policy that was always followed by the Conservatives?
The bill he has now introduced is again devised so as to take the teeth out of a piece of Liberal legislation.
In 1951-52, important amendments were introduced to give effect to the MacQuarrie report. Again the Conservatives fought those amendments tooth and nail, and among their main speakers, there was the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill)-the most misquoted minister of the cabinet-the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough), the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), a former minister without portfolio. Discussion of the bill lasted six days. In other words, the Conservatives fought for at least six days against the amendments introduced in 195152. And they did not just make speeches, oh no. The present Minister of Justice in 1951, suggested a six months' hoist; the leader of the C.C.F. had moved an amendment "for public control of resale price maintenance", and the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration moved an amendment to Mr. 

Coldwell's proposal. Mr. Drew, then Conservative leader suggested that the consideration of the bill be deferred until the supreme court had ruled on the constitutional validity of the act.
Amendments were put forward to keep the discussion going and to stretch out the debate against the proposed piece of legislation.
And when it came to the third reading, Mr. Drew, the Conservative leader-therefore leader of the present Minister of Justice-again suggested a six months' hoist. Everyone knows that this means killing the bill. Indeed, even in the current discussion- to which the present Minister of Justice has contributed at some length-he said this, as recorded on page 2110 and 2111 of Hansard for 1951:
(Text):
Yet it is positively a dangerous and improper piece of legislation to be enacting now because of the threat it presents to the existence and welfare of the small independent retailer.
... it will accomplish nothing more effective than to increase the power and competitive advantages of the large chain and department stores at the expense of the small retailers.
(Translation):
It was thrilling to hear the minister say such fine words, as if he did not know that chain stores are better able to defend themselves than the small retailer. Chain stores, with a capital of several million dollars, can profusely advertise on television and the radio, as well as in the press. They have the capital to do so. Could they not thus more easily come into conflict with the law than if the small retailer is allowed to use his goods for publicity purposes?
Indeed, I recall that when I was working in my father's store, in the off-season of the year, that is, in January and February, as well as in July and August-goods had to be offered at a lower price to attract customers and get the necessary money to stay in business and pay the employees' wages. That was a necessity. And in the ladies wear trade, it is well known that if the businessman does not get rid of his stock in less than a month's time, he is sure to have it on his hands for another season. Now, as fashion changes frequently, he often has to sell his goods at half price, thus losing money.
That is what the minister wanted to uphold; he wanted to deny those people the right to put on such sales. Now, we, in the Liberal party, are opposed to that. We say that such practice

legitimately giving a man the right to think for himself and by himself in his own business set-up, without disturbing his neighbour, must be maintained. And the minister stated, as recorded on page 2116:
(Text):
The next consideration is that we have no positive evidence that price maintenance has a harmful effect on the consumer with respect to prices.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, that is what he says, but he has no evidence to that effect; it is a mere statement that has to be taken at its face value. Besides, I will show in a moment that those are not the views held by experts.
And, according to page 2117, he is reported to have said:
(Text):
-such evidence as we have not only fails to establish that price maintenance has an adverse effect upon the consumer with regard to prices, or an adverse physical effect upon prices: but that there is evidence that establishes quite conclusively that it will have little or no effect in reducing the cost of living, if outlawed: ...
-we are in no position to determine whether or not it hurts the consumer.
(Translation):
You see, a moment ago he was saying: that has no effect whatever on trade; and now, here, he says that there is no evidence that this may have an effect on trade. Well, he should agree with himself if he does not agree with others; and he should find out whether that may have an effect or not.
According to page 2126, he is recorded to have said:
(Text):
The evidence before us shows that, though there is a restriction on competition in one way. that is vertically, in effect there is created a greater and more effective competition between manufacturers and retailers of competing lines.
(Translation):
There is a lot more I could quote, Mr. Speaker, were I not running short of time. Let me add only this. Section 4 of the famous MacQuarrie report states on page 79 of the French version:
Although precise information is lacking, there is some evidence that resale price maintenance contributes to price stability but that the general level of prices, thus stabilized, is higher than it would be under competitive conditions and production more unstable.
Those words are to be found in the MacQuarrie report, the very report quoted by the Minister of Justice. Farther on, concerning an investigation made by Mr. Oxenfeldt, the following statement is to be found: 79951-0-277
Combines Investigation Act
... when resale price maintenance became effective, it forced chain stores to increase their prices, while individual drug stores, on the average, showed price reductions which, however, varied considerably with the size of stores, and, for all independent store groups, the percentage decreases shown were much less than the percentage increases made by chain stores.
Those were the findings. They brought about price increases and the public and the consumer had to foot the bill.
The following is to be found under section 2:
The price increases were greatest in large cities and in large stores.
And farther down:
.. . the stores that reduced their prices ... were not the stores that had been charging the highest prices: The reduction in the price spread was accomplished through compulsory increase from the lowest previous price.
You have there research carried out by serious economists who knew their business, and that investigation on price maintenance legislation was made not only in the United States but throughout the world. Having completed such a thorough investigation, the same economists gave evidence before the commissions, to the effect that price maintenance brings about price increases, which in turn are borne by the consumer and give rise to inflation. And this is exactly what this government is trying to do through this bill. The present Minister of Finance expressed the same opinion and the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said in 1951, as shown on page 2167 of Hansard:
(Text):
We will undoubtedly have a raid on name brands.
We will have a race for the lowest price...
I contend that this legislation is a blind...
(Translation):
And now, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that, when speaking of a "raid on name brands" we actually refer to those we have seen. And who is doing this? The large corporations are. For instance, the large corporations are asking coffee firms to package a special brand for them. It is exactly the same product as the others are getting but they sell it 10 cents cheaper, while the small retailer may not reduce the price of a known brand without running the risk of the producer refusing to sell it to him.
To my mind, such practice is immoral and unfair. And the Minister of Justice should have thought twice before introducing his amendment. The Minister of Transport said the same thing, and so did the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
It can be easily seen that the greatest worry of the Conservatives is to oppose special prices, for advertising purposes, which

Combines Investigation Act benefit the people at large. But what is being done today aims at the same purpose by indirect means.
When pretending that this practice is detrimental to small retailers, they fail to consider that the larger establishments, the chain stores, have had their own packaging made that they can sell at a better price, thus attracting customers at the expense of the small shopkeeper.
In 1951, amendments were submitted to a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, and the Minister of Justice stated last night that amendments introduced in 1951 and 1952, had been passed in a hurry. Now, the MacQuarrie commission, which was appointed in 1950, seriously delved into the matter. After having submitted its report, a joint committee of both houses was formed in order to reconsider the matter. And it was only after passing all these tests, that the bill was introduced in a practical form in this house by the Liberal party. However, at the time, it was criticized by the present Minister of Justice who was formerly the official critic for the opposition.
As the Leader of the Opposition said, we see a real danger in the definitions under section 32, because they are conceived in such a way as to allow, by devious means, what the present act prohibits. Many a thing can be accomplished by an exchange of statistics; by a definition of standards for various products; by an exchange of information on credits. And that is an entirely unfair and immoral thing. They even go as far as to set up what is called a "black list" for certain people who for some reason refused to pay their accounts. They are dragged into court because they are on the list of those considered to be in bad standing, and that is where human conscience is being tampered with, because, being black listed, they are prevented from receiving certain products from particular manufacturers.
Then, there is the definition of terms with regard to trade; there is co-operation in the field of research and development; restriction of publicity and, finally, everything that is not mentioned under paragraph 3. This act is really planned to be bad. And the Minister of Justice, being a lawyer, knows quite well that not a court in the world would accept such an ill drafted and incomprehensible text as this; "All that is not enumerated in subsection 3". This is actually the draft that was recommended in 1950 by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and which was opposed by the Liberal party; and it is Conservative government, which seemingly to help the small businessmen, serves the purposes of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
[Mr. Caron.l
On this matter, here is what Mr. Myron W. Watkins had to say in "Monopoly and Free Enterprise".
(Text):
Trade associations frequently engage in a variety of activities some of which are perhaps innocent or even wholesome when considered separately but which together tend to curb competition and restrain trade. Standardization of products and cost accounting methods, for example, may eliminate waste and lower costs, but it also helps ensure uniform prices among trade rivals. Exchange of information on the credit of customers may help reduce bad debts, but it may also serve as a basis for boycotting "undesirable" customers. Statistical reporting on prices, output, sales, shipment, stocks and the like may aid producers in independently formulating sound price and production policies, but it may also afford a basis for a tacit understanding to stabilize prices and curtail output.
(Translation):
And I could quote even more if time permitted. It is clearly established by economists themselves that the theories enunciated yesterday and in 1951 by the present Minister of Justice, as well as those enunciated by Mr. Bennett and Mr. Meighen, were false and had no value in the face of facts. And if we consider them in the light of the facts, they fall of themselves.
Mr. Speaker, what a situation it will create for our judges. As in the past, they will have to determine the existence of an agreement and of the degree of control, but furthermore, when agreements are related to certain things like the exchange of statistics, the definition of products standards, etc., how do you expect our judges who are probably legal lights but not economists, and who do not have certain agencies available to them to investigate and find out exactly what there is in this or that matter, to be able to pass judgments in such cases and in such conditions? I suggest that the minister, since he is a lawyer, should have known the difficulty in which he was placing the judges.
If we compare the new clause 12, section 31 of the act, with clause 17(4), we note that too extensive discretionary powers are given to the Attorney General of Canada. He will be able to prosecute as he pleases under criminal or common law. What is dangerous for a politician would not be so for a statesman. How many statesmen are there in the present government?
Far from me the thought that the present Minister of Justice would use his powers in one way for party friends and in another way for opponents. Nevertheless, I should like to keep him away from temptation. More

than any other he knows that Christ said: "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak".
It might be said that he has principles and is well-intentioned, but let us not forget either the saying: "The road to hell is paved with good intentions".
I should not want to see the minister reduced to that. I should like him to wake up in order to hear clearly the judgment that is being passed on his legislation, so that he will not find himself in an inferior situation under the pressures exerted by politicians, by party supporters, by interested parties. In spite of all his good intentions, in spite of his honesty, the minister finds himself in an awkward situation brought about by himself, and that should not be.
Instead, he should do as in the past, when the chairman of the royal commission was instructed to make investigations, to offer suggestions to the government, and to submit a report that was brought before the house and made available to government as well as opposition members.
He would thus be protected, as he would realize that the opposition is watching him closely. But, as things stand, the opposition is unable to keep a close watch over his actions, for he is the only one responsible for decisions to be taken at the civil or at the criminal level. The danger lies in the fact that he is sole judge in the matter.
He can bring in indictments through informers who supply information to the minister and he is then in a position to use his discretionary power.
Now, if you look at section 5 closely you find that matters are even worse. Six informers can demand an investigation. Do you realize what that means, Mr. Speaker?
Is it not possible for a large chain store to direct six of its employees to act as informers against another chain store, and is it not possible for the latter to do the same against some other such store? It is so easy, when a law is so made up that it may apply upon mere information, whether it be justified or not.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is bad, that we cannot accept it, that the government has no right to present the Canadian people with legislation thus constructed.
Mr. Speaker, I regret, but I have to go on to another item, since my time is limited.
79951-0-277J
Combines Investigation Act As regards the offence, here is what we find in the bill:
Where the offence Is with respect to a merger or monopoly-
The minister forgot to define what should be understood by a merger; in fact, there may be several kinds of mergers. Some are bad and some are good; some are necessary and some are dangerous.
Here is an example of a necessary merger.
It will be recalled that around 1920, the Banque Nationale found itself in serious financial trouble, while the Banque d'Hoche-laga also experienced some difficulties, though to a lesser degree. So the Quebec government forced a merger of the two banks under the name of Banque Canadienne Nationale; the government guaranteed a $25 million loan, and thus protected the depositors and shareholders, both large and small. Today, the Banque Canadienne Nationale is a strong institution and compares favourably with any other bank, precisely because of that merger and of the Quebec government's backing.
The Banque Canadienne Nationale was thus a case of necessary merger, and it lead to a very happy result, because it is now a great banking institution, one of the most prosperous in Canada.
That point is not covered in the bill. The bill only refers to mergers. A merger as such is not a bad thing. I think the minister has overlooked that point.
I see that my time is running out, so I shall have to cut short. Let me only say that this legislation is a threat to the general public, that it is inflationary in nature, that it gives the minister too much arbitrary power, and finally that it may lead to serious inequities.
Here is my credo:
I would hope the combines legislation would grant equal opportunities to all, whether big or small. It should grant the small or average businessman the right to buy the products which he resells at a price as favourable as that of his competitors.
The right to buy on a free market products which will be resold on a free market.
The right to fix his prices to meet competition from all quarters.
The right to administer his own business according to his own judgment.
I ask those things for the small businessmen because they alone need the constant protection of the authorities. As for the big,

For all those reasons, I will vote against this bill on second reading.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we believe that this is a bad bill in that it introduces amendments that will further weaken or debilitate an act that is none too effective at the present time.
The minister entertained me, and I am sure he must have entertained other hon. members on this side of the house-I do not know about his own following; they were a little tardy in their ability to applaud but that may not have any significance-with a number of things. One thing that I found very interesting was his predilection to the phrase "Conservative principles" with which he interlarded and interlaced his speech. I could not quite make out from his remarks whether these amendments indicate that the Conservative principles are for the encouragement of big business or for the protection and encouragement of small business. I might say the reason anyone who feels he is a socialist or socialistically inclined has to take an interest in combines because it raises a fundamental question to anyone who considers that the government or the state has to and is bound to, with the trend of the times, play a larger and larger role, not necessarily in enterprise but in the regulatory field.
In talking about the mid-twentieth century and adjusting this act to the times I think the minister has really set the keynote of what we should be speaking about and yet he has done very little to elaborate on just how these amendments fit, and how the wholesale revision that he merely prefigured would fit into the mid-twentieth century.
He dealt with the question of bigness in a most vague and indefinite way. He said the Conservative government-at least this is my paraphrase of it, Mr. Speaker-was not against big business; it did not necessarily believe that big business was good or was necessarily more efficient. Now, we have been fighting a campaign against and for big business, and when I say "we" I mean it has been in the climate of opinion in North America for at least 60 years, the question of big business and whether it is good or bad. It has had a bad reputation among many people, especially just before the first war and during the depression. When the


minister talks about the mid-twentieth century one cannot help wonder why he does not face up the situation we have in Canada today-this is even more striking than in the United States, of very huge businesses and corporations getting larger and larger and consolidating and concentrating more and more.
I can illustrate this very well from the economy of my own region which tends to be an isolated one. It is based primarily upon the manufacture of newsprint and various pulp and paper products. We have a large kraft or sulphate mill in Marathon. This was United States capital when it first came in, a relatively small company by United States standards, certainly. It was capitalized near $100 million in its total operation and about two years ago it found difficulties, I believe in raising capital for expansion. The first thing we knew was that our Marathon mill had become part of a much larger framework, one of the mightiest of all corporations in the United States, the American Can Company.
The mill just to the west of that, Long Lac Paper Company, has been part of a large concern, Kimberley-Clark, famous for its manufacture of a product that we all know and use, namely Kleenex. I am not giving it a plug here but I think hon. members all realize from the ubiquitousness of that particular article the scale of the operation that that particular mill and associated woods production fits into.
The next mill along the way once belonged to Brompton. Actually, it got under way just before the second war, in the hands of one of Canada's colourful and most reputable robber barons, Bob Sweezey-I think you will agree with that term-a gentleman who first became mixed up in the Beauharnois scandal and later on in a number of other financial affairs. Brompton Paper Company picked up the Red Rock paper mill when it was broke as a result of the kind of overcapitalization and promotion that happened in pulp and paper companies just before the war. Since then it has moved into the hands of the St. Lawrence Corporation; recently it became part of the managerial enterprise of a man who is very well known, almost a symbol of big business in this country, E. P. Taylor.
Further along the coast, in Fort William, we have a paper mill that has the largest newsprint machines in the world, Great Lakes. It has had a very vigorous kind of expansion recently. At one time it was under the presidency of the hon. member for Duf-ferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), and we considered it a local enterprise. It had its head office at the lakehead. It still has its head office at the lakehead, but we now know that very

recently it too has moved into this very huge complex of pulp and paper companies that Mr. Taylor has under his control.
To the west we have Dryden Paper, which again started fairly small and has since moved up until it is a very large part of the Anglo-Canadian empire; and so it goes, with almost all of our mills. I almost inadvertently forgot to mention that we have three mills at the lakehead which are controlled by Abitibi Power and Paper Company which was in bankruptcy during the depression and has since fought its way out of it and now has mills in operation across Canada and recently extended its operations into the United States. It is a Canadian goliath.
The point I am making about all these companies and their tendency to grow bigger is that it almost seems inevitable that the trend in this particular field, where such large scale capitalization is necessary, is toward hugeness. I want to underline that in our part of the country we have nothing against these companies because they are big, but I should like to look at some of the consequences of their very bignesses. Some of these companies like Marathon and Ontario Minnesota have as much as 2,000 square miles of forest country. They have literally taken over the field from the small woods operator. Today we no longer have the host of small contractors, or the middling size, who were able to move around and obtain certain areas of wood and exploit them in any way, shape or form. As a matter of fact, we have had a very marked decline in that kind of family enterprise and the situation now is that the pulp and paper companies in their dealings with people who have wood that is not on their own property deal with very small farmers or what we might call bush settlers. From a forest management view this may be good. I think it is worth while knowing that, especially when we look at the combines report of the restrictive trade practices commission in dealing with the subject of pulpwood in certain districts in eastern Canada. This report is an indication of how the small individual farmer or wood cutter is treated, in the face of the kind of combination that this pulp and paper industry can create.
Beyond the fact that we have these very large corporations exploiting the forests, giving us a great deal of employment and, incidentally, providing the very large export value that Canada has, we find them cooperating in a number of ways.
For example, we have one co-operative research program, RC-17, in which the Ontario government, the federal government, Abitibi, Ontario Paper and a whole host of other people and agencies, including the
Combines Investigation Act northwestern Ontario timber operators and groups like that, have worked together for research purposes. This is what the minister has indicated he is effecting in the bill. We are at the stage now that if anyone wants to work in the bush in any sort of long term way and with any chance of security of employment and any kind of promotion in the future, to think of doing it himself on his own and through his own resources according to the old traditional idea of the eager entrepreneur is nonsense. It is silly for any young person today to think of founding his own enterprise in the bush. It is almost hopeless. He cannot get capital, he cannot get training, he cannot get experience, he cannot get wood. What he has to do is become part of one of these very large organizations. This is what has happened within the past 20 or 25 years in our major basic industry in that region.
If we look at other aspects of our economy, what are we faced with? We are a major transportation area in Canada. We are the bridge across which everything going east or west has to move. What do we find there? We have two large railroads, the two largest corporations in Canada, I believe, Canadian Pacific and Canadian National, in the transportation field. We have very large air lines such as Trans-Canada providing through service and so far as smaller air line service is concerned we have noted a tendency to consolidate. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has had protests recently at the opening up of this field to more people who are coming in on a small scale. It has been argued rather effectively that this opening up of the field to other individuals is killing off the people already established in the small air line business.
When the C.P.R. moved into Smith Transport and as the railways developed the piggyback service what else have we noticed? There has been a marked drop in the number of trucking operators giving through service. The piggy-back service offered by the railways and the moving of the railways into this field of transportation has cut down and is going to continue to cut down markedly the number of truckers in the business. In other words, we are again moving toward greater size and consolidation, toward the requirement of greater capital and a situation where there are fewer and fewer opportunities for the small person to get going and to get anywhere. The trucking association has made very strong protests in various places against this trend of the railways moving into the trucking field. I see that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) is here. He has been a spokesman in this regard.

Combines Investigation Act
The irony of the situation is that the railways have no difficulty at all in buying up trucking firms. In other words, despite the ethos that dictates that you should start small and build up a going small enterprise, trucking presidents and managers of firms are quite ready to sell out at an advantageous price, allowing this field to develop into bigger and bigger consolidations around these two pillars of Canadian transport, the C.P.R. and the Canadian National. That is the situation in the two main basic industries.
In our third industry, mining, what do we find. We have a very interesting development north of Port Arthur at Nakina where Anaconda Copper, a colossus in world copper, has given every indication that it is going to move in and spend almost a billion dollars in developing a huge iron ore trench which is anywhere from 40 to 60 miles in scope. It is fantastic to think of a small man or a small operator in that kind of field. The main developed mine that we have in our area, Steep Rock, belongs to the Cyrus Eaton interests and hon. members all know the ramifications of his empire. He has dickerings in Greenland, dickerings in Ungava, relationships with the Russians, relationships with the Germans. It is truly an international organization of great scope and size.
I would not argue that there are not opportunities for young men in such an organization, but in a field such as this, the development of this basic resource that means so much to our area and our country's prosperity, the idea of a role for the small person is nonsensical. More and more we can see that it is a case of immense funds handled by immense and huge corporations.
When you turn to other aspects of mining you find that what might be called the best mine in my constituency, Geco, which has a smart management and a magnificent ore body, was discovered by a couple of very small prospectors. They are getting a good return from it as a result of the deal they made but in effect Geco is an offshoot of Noranda which is one of the largest of all mining outfits in Canada. If any hon. members follow the Northern Miner I am sure they are aware that in the years especially since the war there has been a great consolidation in the mining field. Managerial groups have developed and they have made a tremendous contribution in one way in the Red Lake area by taking over mines that were considered dead, putting a lot of money into them, driving these mines to depth and finding and developing large ore bodies. Again the situation in the mining field is like that in the pulp and paper field and in the transportation field. You have larger and larger units

with more and more a managerial revolution based on large capital and advanced techniques which is complete in one sense in that the small man no longer has a place except as an employee.
It used to be considered in our part of the country that prospecting was one of the last endeavours where there would always be scope for the individual prospector. We still have some prospectors but in many cases they are disillusioned because in competing against large corporations which can afford to hire aeromagnetic service and send out specialists such as geologists and even assay people with the prospecting party the ordinary small prospector has not much of a chance.
When we look in our region at what has been traditionally a field of opportunity for the small scale concern, the retail business, we see what has happened to three large local family enterprises. I am thinking of the Chappies', Matthews' and Bryans' stores. I say they were large because their sales volume was in the millions. They had a great many local employees and family managements. But what has happened? Chappies was sold to Great-West Saddlery which, operating out of Winnipeg and having the capital, is building up a chain of stores in that part of the country. I believe that Matthews was sold to Eatons and that Bryans was sold to Simpsons-Sears, although I may be wrong there. But here again the big retail outlets in our area are Simpsons-Sears and Eatons, national organizations.
The grocery field has been preempted by Safeway, Loblaws and A & P. We have had a very marked decline in small grocery stores, and some of them were not so small. They were quite substantial. But in most cases they have been forced to give up growth prospects and in many cases have had to go out of business. So our people shop mainly at the very large supermarkets that have mushroomed across the country since the war. There is no gainsaying this trend. It is obvious throughout the country; it is obvious in Ottawa.
Then there is the situation in the service type of industry. I am thinking of cleaners and dyers, garages and operations of that type. Again it is very difficult for the small man to operate. If he is in existence it is more and more the case that he is a lessee on a very doubtful and shaky basis from a large organization. Most automobile repairs and that type of thing are now tied in with the larger franchise holders of the big manufacturers.
As to the construction industry, one would expect that in a country with the amount of space that we have and very severe winter

conditions construction development would be improving. What we find is that the small contractors are not proliferating. Instead of having more and more small contractors, we are getting fewer and fewer big ones. Indeed, the irony is that it is almost impossible for any of our local contractors to make a successful bid on a government project, for example, because they cannot compete with the lower bids of the huge organizations with headquarters in Toronto, Winnipeg and centres like that.
One cannot argue against the trend. The trend is there. We can see it. But it seems to me that what we should really do is analyse how big is big, and whether we should let this bigness go any farther, whether there are certain fields in which we should allow this trend and other fields in which we should stop it. Should we set a limit on the size of corporations? I think, perhaps, even more realistic than the type of control we get from the combines act would be a corporate graduated income tax which might do more to control this movement toward huge size, if it is worth controlling.
One of the things that intrigued me in reviewing this legislation was the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), with all deference to his Conservative principles about the history of this legislation. I think the real builder and founder of this legislation was the Right Hon. Mackenzie King. Speaking on the original bill in 1910 Mr. King said:
Broadly viewed, It is in the machinery for investigation and for the framing and shaping of an intelligent public opinion which the measure provides, that its main features consist. It aims to get at the truth and to have the truth when ascertained so presented that the remedy for a wrong disclosed will be self-evident. It is framed in the belief that once in possession of the facts which are of first importance to itself, the public will find a way of seeing that any evil under which it may be wrongfully suffering will be removed and that no situation, however complicated, will prove too intricate for a satisfactory solution, but to ascertain the facts, to get at the truth, is the first of all essentials.
It seems to me that Mr. King was very optimistic. He had a great belief that if the public only knew, if the public only realized and saw some examples of combines and mergers and price fixing, the public would so react that this trend would be wiped out. What we are faced with, I would suggest to the minister in the mid-twentieth century, is a fait accompli. We have huge corporations. I am not suggesting they are combines in the nasty sense of the word. I am not suggesting they are the result of mergers in the criminal sense of the word. However, the fact remains that we have them. I wonder just what we should be doing in legislative
Combines Investigation Act terms in order to halt the trend or to reverse the trend. It certainly seems to me that what the minister is trying to do in one part of this act is, in many ways, to make it easier for big business to get bigger, and at the same time he has thrown out a sop to small business in so far as this resale price maintenance tendency is concerned which is supposed to please them.
The minister argued that there is a place for the small businessman. We would not argue against this, but I think he needs to defend his argument against this trend of the times, as I have pointed out and which is so obvious in our particular part of the country. There is always the argument of economies of scale. How can a small businessman really compete with these large scale enterprises that are able to supply cheaper buys and better service? In the long run, despite all the talk about bigger or smaller business, I believe the only way we will retain small business, especially in the retail field and in the service field, is by deliberately stopping the expansion into larger groups.
This raises the question of efficiency and relative efficiency. Here again, we do not know. Perhaps instead of these amendments being put in front of a parliamentary committee it might have been better if they had gone before this royal commission that we have not got but could have had if the minister had been as serious, as we think he should have been.
The difficulty in so far as small business in industrial fields is concerned, aside from the retail stores, although the difficulty appears there as we know, is the raising of capital. We have had one election campaign fought to a degree upon the question of tight money. Outside the house the minister has indicated that the new small business bureau is going to be one means of answering the problem of small business and the small manufacturer. I suggest to him that so far it has been an organizational agency only, or a minor promotional agency. It still has not got around to the role that is being played by the small business administration in the United States, under which large loans are available at relatively low interest rates. There the loans are relatively large, up to $300,000 or $400,000 on a long term basis.
We have not anything like that from this government that would indicate it really is out to do something for the small manufacturer, the young man with some ideas and perhaps a bit of technical ability who wants to get ahead. As it is now, the young man with technical skill and drive almost certainly has to find his role within a very large

Combines Investigation Act organization. I do not know whether I mentioned this before in the house, but I remember a few years ago at a university at which I worked there were 27 boys in one graduating class in commerce. There was not one of them going into business on his own or even thinking about it. Every one of them signed with a very large organization. I have tried to trace some of them since, and what I have been able to discover from a partial sampling has been that most of them are doing very well in large organizations such as Standard Oil of New Jersey, Imperial Oil and very large accountancy firms.
What I am trying to argue, Mr. Speaker, and reiterate and reiterate, is that we have this tremendous trend today. Even geologists in our particular area have gotten together to form a firm so that they could take on the size and kind of projects that are necessary. Except with dentists and lawyers you can see a trend toward some kind of co-operation in the professional field. This is apparent throughout our whole society. All hon. members have observed how, more and more, doctors are moving into clinics. I know in our particular area most of the medical work is done through clinics of a fairly large size. As a matter of fact, the largest clinic is on a share basis, just like a company, and declares dividends and has profits. Again I am not making any comment as to the worth of this trend, but this is the trend of the times, even in the medical field, of having more and more employees with less and less opportunity for the small person, the family doctor, the small family enterprise.
It needs to be mentioned in this debate, it seems to me, that one of the developments about which many people, not the least of whom are on the government side, are wailing about is the trend in the trade union movement. This might be one logical answer to this trend of corporate bigness. You might say it has been one of the countervailing powers against their development in size. If we have huge unions, such as the united steelworkers with their scope in the United States and throughout Canada, this is a reflection of the very large scale of the industries in which employees work. The big forces of our time in our economy are big corporations tending to be bigger all the time, and also big unions tending to be bigger all the time.
It seems to me that if we want to return to what is largely a myth we have to come out with very firm rules and restrictions against the increase in the size of corporations or of unions. We need to get some definitions of bigness and of smallness. We

need to get some definitions of efficiency before we treat things so haphazardly as the minister has treated them in this particular piece of legislation.
One of the points that the minister made was his indication that the government had not received any representations from the manufacturers in connection with the list price policy that section 34 prohibits. He said that in the main the government had followed the representations of small business. I do not know whether he has followed the campaign of the Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Limited which has a public relations office in Toronto. Sunbeam, right across the country, working as I understand it with the retail merchants association, has put the case strongly for price maintenance; and in effect that is what the minister has given. With all due respect to the retail merchants association I think we deserve a more candid and a more thorough analysis of just what this is going to do actually to protect the small businessman and also to protect him from the manufacturer with whom he will tend to be tied.
By hon. members who have already spoken the point has been made about protecting the consumer in so far as the price setting aspect of these amendments goes. It seems to me that the consumer always is forgotten in our part of the world as a political entity. I think this is probably a factor in all three of the political parties in this house. I think we may tend to make a fetish of the small businessman because of the myth we have. To underline this I want to read some remarks from a recent book by a Canadian economist, B. S. Keirstead and entitled "Capital Interest and Profits". In this book he states as follows:
Western peoples have given much lip service to the ideal of free private enterprise. Such a system is supposed to create the optimum output of goods and services and is believed to be continuously progressive because of competition. Competition is also believed to protect the public against exploitation and to ensure that abnormal profits would be ephemeral. To ensure competition. laws have been passed making monopolies, trusts, mergers, combines and price agreements illegal. Yet one wonders how much of all this is a kind of elaborate social mythology. A truly competitive world is one in which some people get hurt. The inefficient producer goes into bankruptcy; farmers who fail to alter acreage in response to price changes cannot sell their crops. Workers in declining trades have to take lower wages, go unemployed or move to other trades and other areas. By contrast with this harsh world is our kindly paternalistic North American society. If American (or Canadian) manufacturers are suffering from foreign competition, up go the tariffs. If farmers grow too much wheat or make too much butter to sell at the price they want, the government buys it at an agreed price in excess of the market price. If coal from submarginal Cape Breton mines cannot be sold at a profit, subventions are paid to move the coal at less than cost to the Montreal market. If there is serious unemployment and poverty in Newfoundland, we

do not allow starvation to drive the people out,
i.e. increase labour mobility; we pay a special subsidy to Newfoundland. It may be that all this is as it should be; it is not free private enterprise.
This argument, it seems to me, must throw us back upon an analysis of the situation we have today, and I reiterate what I started with, namely the questions as to how big is big, how small is small business or how high is small business and how do you determine whether a business is efficient. We can see that obviously big business on the economic side is transforming society. I do not know about the other members of the house but it has certainly altered my habits with regard to shopping, how I drive and where I drive. It has certainly altered employment opportunities for me and for most of the people that I know.
It seems to me that we have had a transformation of society, yet we do not face up to it. We still keep talking, as does the minister, about free private enterprise and Conservative principles which are always going to see that that ideal is maintained. I tend to feel that this situation is rather long past and that tinkering in the way in which the minister seems to be tinkering here can do nothing but raise suspicion in our minds as to the short run motive of the minister and of the government.
When I speak of suspicion, I wonder how he can spend three years, as he says, in intensive study. We almost have a picture of him, Mr. MacDonald and the other people over at the combines investigation section, day after day churning away at this thing, threading through the MacQuarrie report and looking over the whole field: they are really set to go; they are really drawing things up; they are going to change it. But what has actually happened? The minister introduces his speech by saying that these are not revisions, that this is not a revision of the act and not to be mistaken for it; that these are only relatively minor amendments that are not going to change the purpose of the act but are going to deal with certain specific situations. If small business is in a quandary, surely this act needs something more important than the minister's minor amendments. If we have a situation in which big business is getting bigger all the time and we are getting corporate consolidation all the time, surely after three years we need something more than his way of making the act more ineffectual.
I hope later on, after amendments have been moved with regard to this particular bill, to have the opportunity of coming down to more specific criticism of the bill. However, I felt that the whole issue of bigness and size in our business structure was worthy 79951-0-278
Combines Investigation Act of some examination. If corporations continue to get bigger-and I know there are limits within certain fields-it obviously means that there are going to be fewer and fewer of them in the field. Perhaps we should be considering ways of making sure that the few which are in the field compete rather than adopting this ineffectual way of making it easier for them to combine.
In conclusion I should like to ask the minister to remember this pulpwood combines report. If the minister studies it he will find that these extremely large organizations that co-operate-at least I think they co-operate- in these appeals that are before the courts at the present time are linked with the pulp and paper research institute of Canada which is subsidized heavily by the Canadian government. They are linked with the Canadian pulp and paper association which has a woodland section which interchanges information and research in which government scientists and foresters spend a great deal of time and in which there is interchange of information, statistics and facts. We even have a situation, in so far as the pulp and paper wood side is concerned, where one of the government agencies produced an economic survey of costs on a certain pulp and paper watershed.
This type of co-operation that we have in this largest industrial field we have in Canada indicates to me that the time has been reached when we need to go into this question of bigness and corporate association in all its aspects much more thoroughly than the minister has suggested. He spoke as though his legislation was going to open the oportunity for co-operative research. It is obvious that in the pulp and paper industry that situation exists at the present time in many aspects. It seems to me that his motives, in so far as this legislation is concerned, are not going to do anything for the control of big business. They are not going to do anything effective for the support of small business. Again we carry on with the myth, the blarney, the typical political solution of trying to appeal to every field we possibly can without being crystal clear.
If the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) had the courage in effect to tell the housing industry to go jump in the lake and if the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had the courage to tell A. V. Roe to go jump in the lake as far as the Arrow is concerned, I suggest to the Minister of Justice that he should consider telling big business or small business to jump in some lake. But I do not see how he can have it that he is pulling them both out of the lake at the same time. It seems to me there is a conflict here and

Combines Investigation Act that either one or the other is going to drown. There has to be something done immediately in other fields if we are to have the ideal situation where those Conservative principles reign about which he talks so sweetly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped some of the government members would rise to speak on this matter and that they would have endorsed not what the minister said but what they think the minister said, that is that he supported their views that we should maintain big business or that we are pledged to this legislation to support small business.
Frankly I would like to know where the Conservative party stands on this. Are they for small business or big business? I was listening to the minister yesterday and I think it would be very difficult to say whether he was for the small businessman or for big business. It appears to me that there is very little similarity in the needs and desires of these two organizations.
I can say without any consideration of the matter that I am not particularly interested in big business. I do not care about legislation to assist big business. I do not particularly want to eliminate big business because I think it is able to look after themselves. I want to support legislation which will allow small businesses to operate and will allow them to have at least a fair and equal opportunity of existence, which is not true at the present time.
In my own home town in the last few months we have had two businesses go out of business. One was a very large factory, probably the largest woodworking plant in Canada today and certainly the most modern, Hill-Clark-Francis. It has been known for years to be one of the leading manufacturers of fabricated wood products, but a few months ago it decided to all intents and purposes to close its doors. This factory was a large one employing 300, 400 and sometimes 500 people. It was a plant which had attached to it many retail outlets in northern Ontario. They owned the Halliday Lumber Company of Burlington and other lumber companies in British Columbia and throughout the country. They closed their doors and did not make any bones about saying that it was because of competition, or for other reasons. Now they are willing to use other people for their supplies.
At the same time, while this is very much a disadvantage to the town in an employment sense, a small business was started up several years ago which had a very capable manager, a capable staff, and was serving a need in the community and was in the position of a small business. It was a small business connected very closely with the Conservative


party. The manager of this business was very closely connected with the party in my riding and only a few months ago this business folded up.
It seems to me that there must be a much more effective way of allowing these small businesses not to have an advantage over big business but to be able to compete with them. I have examined many of the procedures used in big business and I find that they are very dishonest procedures. You can go to any small businessman who will object most violently over your being able to walk down the street and find a sign in a tobacco store or in a large supermarket which says that cigarettes are sold for $3.18 a carton when the wholesale price of the same people who supply them to the supermarket is $3.19 to the small businessman. Each one of these small businessmen objects most violently, not because he is not able to compete in the sense of operating his business efficiently but in the sense that he is not able to buy in equal competition because there is a combine in the wholesale industry which allows the wholesaler to sell to their own particular outlets at one price, to a volume outlet at another price, and to the small retailer at yet a third, fourth or fifth price in many cases.
These matters are matters of concern to every small businessman. I am sure that each member of the House of Commons has received many petitions in the last few months and I would like to read one which comes from a small store in my area that is not interested in competing with large wholesale outlets, and is not interested in competing even with the large supermarket because there is not one in his community. This man has a store in a small community and has been able to increase the size of his store and put in those additions which will make him a kind of small supermarket where he is giving service and the best product possible to his customers. I will not read what the petition says because all hon. members have received this, but he says:
Today when competition demands larger stores, modern equipments and a large variety of merchandise, the small merchants are at a real disadvantage to compete with the large corporate chains. Chains have a ready source of finances from the public through sales of stocks, debentures etc., whereas the only moneys available to the small merchant is a very limited and inadequate credit from the banks and his small profits which makes it just about impossible to expand.
We are also definitely against trading stamps. In spite of all statements to the contrary, stamps are costly, 2 per cent and sometimes more and if they are legalized there is no doubt that all merchants will be forced to handle them and the cost will be passed on to the consumers.
Loss leaders and discriminatory price practices are also more harmful to the small merchants than the large chains. Since chains by quantity buying pay less for most of their merchandise than the

small merchants unfair trade practices do not hurt them as much as the smaller operator.
It would seem to me that if the Conservatives, and I mean the real Conservatives- not these "Johnny come latelys" who are Diefenbaker Conservatives, who were progressive a few years ago; who decided that John was a progressive and they would go along with him because they think he thinks a certain way-who were for Horatio Alger in the days when Horatio Alger was popular in the United States-
